name: Banff Skatepark
why: A New Line Skateparks build off Sundance Road beside the town's ball diamonds, with a long snake-run bowl (hips, extensions, vert walls, pump bumps) and a street course of hubbas, stairs, handrails, a pole jam and a Euro gap.
heads_up: Open sunrise to sunset; watch for fly balls from the ball diamonds next door and give elk and other wildlife plenty of space.

name: Callingwood Skatepark
why: A 19,500 sq ft New Line Skateparks street park in west Edmonton with granite-topped hubba ledges, stair sets, handrails, gaps, manual pads and a half pipe.
heads_up: Listed hours are sunrise to sunset; it's mostly street terrain, so transition skaters may want to pair it with Castle Downs or Mill Woods.

name: Castle Downs Skatepark
why: A large all-concrete park on 153 Avenue NW beside the Castle Downs YMCA, with a big flow bowl (hips, extension, roller, roll-in and a transfer spine) and a full street course.
heads_up: Open 5 a.m. to 11 p.m.; Edmonton asks skaters to ride only when the surface is dry and free of snow and ice.

name: Cowboys Park Skatepark (formerly Shaw Millennium Park)
why: Opened in 2000 on the west edge of downtown, its 75,000 sq ft of concrete is Canada's largest outdoor skatepark, with street, intermediate and advanced courses, a cloverleaf bowl and a large full pipe. Locals still call it 'Millz' after the Shaw Millennium Park name, which changed to Cowboys Park in 2024.
heads_up: The skatepark is open 24 hours, but some bowls close for the Cowboys Music Festival around Stampede (roughly mid-June to mid-July).

name: Fairview Bike Pump Track
why: Calgary's first asphalt pump track, built in 2020 by Bike Track for the Fairview Community Association, with small tabletops and beginner, intermediate and advanced routes.
heads_up: Parking is limited; don't park in the alley behind Fairview Drive. Open 8 a.m. to 10 p.m.

name: Genesis Centre Skatepark
why: Northeast Calgary's first official skatepark, built by New Line Skateparks in front of the Genesis Centre in Martindale and opened in 2019, with a large bowl and a mostly street layout of hubbas, ledges, rails and stairs.
heads_up: Listed as open 24/7; it sits in front of the Genesis Centre on Falconridge Blvd NE.

name: Glendale Skatepark
why: A New Line Skateparks park of almost 18,000 sq ft with a pool-style bowl, a large flow bowl and street terrain of hubbas, handrails, stair sets, an A-frame ledge and a pole jam, a natural stop on the drive between Edmonton and Calgary.
heads_up: Lit and listed as open 24/7.

name: Huntington Hills Skatepark
why: One of the first three parks built in 2015 under Calgary's skatepark strategy, with a large bowl of extensions, hips, a spine and a pool-style pocket with pool coping, plus hubbas, a handrail, stairs and manual pads.
heads_up: A neighbourhood park at Centre St N and 64 Ave NW, so keep the noise down for the neighbours late in the day.

name: Inglewood Bike Pump Track
why: Opened in October 2021 at 2040 7 Ave S.E., designed by Ground Cubed and Velosolutions: two asphalt tracks for beginner and intermediate riders, just off the Bow River pathway.
heads_up: Free drop-in, 8 a.m. to 10 p.m.

name: Inland Skatepark
why: In Kin Coulee Park below Medicine Hat College, where a 13,500 sq ft addition in 2013 added an upper bowl, a hubba with two rails, and a plaza with a brick bank-to-ledge, a big three-stair, a gap and a warped 'sushi dish' manual pad.
heads_up: It's down the hill from the college on Kipling Street; the older park's terrain sits alongside the 2013 addition.

name: Mill Woods Skatepark
why: One of Edmonton's older parks, by the Mill Woods Recreation Centre, with a bowl of hips, volcanoes and pump bumps and a brick China bank, plus ledges, rails, a Euro gap and a bank-to-bank gap.
heads_up: It's lit and open 24/7, but the older concrete has big cracks, so watch your wheels.

name: New Brighton Skatepark
why: A New Line Skateparks build in southeast Calgary whose bowl has several hips, pocket and vert extensions and a roll-in, next to a street section with two stair sets with handrails, out ledges and a long flat bar.
heads_up: Check the bowl is dry and clear of gravel before dropping in after a storm.

name: South Glenmore Bike Pump Track
why: Velosolutions built two connected asphalt tracks here in 2020, a 110 m beginner loop and a 204 m loop with bigger features, raised above ground because of the high water table by the Glenmore Reservoir.
heads_up: Open 8 a.m. to 10 p.m.; park at 3520 90 Ave S.W. and ride east on the Elbow River pathway.

name: Southwood Skatepark
why: Another of Calgary's 2015 strategy parks, set in a quiet southwest neighbourhood park, with a flow bowl of varying depths and a radial pocket plus ledges, rails, stairs and a bank with an inset ledge.
heads_up: Listed hours are 5 a.m. to 11 p.m.; it's a residential area, so keep it respectful.

name: The Compound Indoor Skatepark
why: Calgary's only indoor skatepark by its own account, run by the Riders on Board snowboard club in a 20,000 sq ft warehouse with a street section, a large mini bowl, flat-ground courts and a beginner area with a 2 ft micro mini.
heads_up: A helmet and a signed waiver are mandatory, and public drop-in runs on set hours, so check the schedule first.

name: West Confederation Bike Pump Track
why: Calgary's newest Velosolutions track, in the southeast corner of West Confederation Park, with a 90 m intermediate loop and a 145 m advanced loop of five berms each.
heads_up: Groups can book it on weekdays; outside bookings it is open for drop-in, 8 a.m. to 10 p.m.

name: Woodlands Skatepark
why: Rebuilt on the old park's site in Legion Memorial Park in 2020, this 14,000 sq ft park has a 5–8 ft pool-style bowl, a 4 ft mini-ramp bowl, a flow bowl with a banked spine and centre island, and a street area.
heads_up: Lights stay on until 11 p.m.; the fenced park's only entrance is on the northeast side, behind the kids' water park.

name: Chilliwack Pump Track
why: Velosolutions built two asphalt tracks at The Landing in late 2020: a pro track of over 300 m with a tunnel, which Velosolutions calls the only one of its kind in North America, and a shorter intermediate track.
heads_up: The pro track is fast and can intimidate young riders; start on the smaller track. Turf edges give softer landings.

name: China Creek Skatepark
why: Vancouver's first skatepark, opened in May 1979 on a filled-in ravine after local skaters worked with a neighbourhood committee on the design. The Vancouver Heritage Foundation named it a Place That Matters in 2022, and the Park Board has been renewing it.
heads_up: No lights, so it's a daylight session; BMX riders share the bowls, so take turns.

name: Chuck Bailey Skatepark
why: About 30,000 sq ft of concrete outside the Chuck Bailey Recreation Centre, mixing a large plaza of ramps, rails and bowls with local art, plus a 5,000 sq ft covered bowl area built for wet-weather riding.
heads_up: Only the covered bowl area stays dry in the rain; the rest of the plaza is open to the weather.

name: Garden City Bike Park
why: Richmond's bike park on Granville Avenue has an obstacle section with skinnies and a teeter-totter, and a dirt jump area with jumps laid out by skill level, from beginner to expert.
heads_up: Dirt jumps: let them dry out after rain.

name: Hastings Park Bike Skills Track
why: In the southeast corner of Hastings Park at the north end of Empire Field: a dirt pump track with sculpted berms, a smaller pump track for kids and wooden skills platforms and ramps.
heads_up: Gets busy in late afternoons; dirt sections need to dry after rain.

name: Hastings Skateboard Park
why: A big concrete park on the west side of Hastings Park, between the PNE Forum and the Italian Gardens, with three connected bowls (the deep end runs about 11 feet) and a small street area. It has hosted contests including the Vans Park Series.
heads_up: Street parking around the PNE grounds is restricted, so use PNE parking; the bowls fill up on dry summer evenings.

name: Inter River Bike Park
why: Opened in 2019 beside a former BMX park, with a BMX dirt jump course, a paved pump track and a dirt pump track. Landyachtz has held timed skateboard races on the paved loop.
heads_up: The jump course is for experienced riders; beginners and intermediates should stick to the pump tracks.

name: Jordie Lunn Bike Park
why: Velosolutions built a 1,500 m² main pump track, a kids' track and a roughly 142 m downhill snake run here in 2020 on a steep site that honours rider Jordie Lunn; the park also has jump and skills zones.
heads_up: The pump tracks have no lights, so plan to ride in daylight.

name: Kamloops Bike Ranch
why: Set up in 2005 inside city limits, the Ranch has jump lines like Tombstone and Wrangler, the floodlit Corral dirt jumps, a BMX track and a new $1.3 million all-wheels pump track.
heads_up: Dirt lines need to dry after rain; a local shuttle (Mostly Mental Shuttles) has run laps to the top.

name: Kensington Skateboard Park
why: A compact East Vancouver park at Knight Street and East 37th Avenue built around a pool-style bowl about 9.5 feet at the deep end and 5 feet at the shallow end, plus a mini-ramp and amphitheatre-style ledges.
heads_up: No lights; the pool bowl is deep for a small park, so newer skaters should warm up on the mini-ramp.

name: Leeside Tunnel Skateboard Park
why: A volunteer-built DIY park inside an abandoned 49 m tunnel under the Cassiar Connector at East Hastings, named for skater and artist Lee Matasi, who was killed in Gastown in 2005. About a dozen hand-built mini-ramps, quarter pipes and grind poles fill the tunnel.
heads_up: Reach it down the lane behind the E-Comm building off East Pender; laneway parking is tight, so park on East Pender and keep the driveways clear.

name: Metro Skate Park (Bonsor Park)
why: Next to Metrotown in Bonsor Park, with a street zone, a bowl zone that includes a full pipe, and a beginner section with a shallow bowl and grind curbs.
heads_up: No lights, so plan a daylight session; beginners have their own shallow-bowl section away from the full pipe.

name: Mountain Air Bike Skills Park
why: Built for mountain bikers on the north side of Burnaby Mountain, with skinnies, elevated bridges, drops, teeter-totters, wood and dirt pump tracks and dirt jumps.
heads_up: Washrooms and picnic tables on site; wooden features get slick in the wet.

name: One Love Indoor Skatepark
why: A non-profit indoor park that opened in October 2021 in a former grocery store in Whalley, run by the faith-based One Love International Society and led by former pro skater Dan Pageau, with wooden ramps, lessons and a skate shop.
heads_up: The wooden ramps get moved around for Sunday services, so the layout and hours change; check before you go.

name: Pemberton Bike Skills Park
why: Opened in 2022 in Den Duyf Park with four zones (pump track, skills park, drop zone and jump lines) rated so riders can progress. It was paid for mostly by a provincial grant of about $974,000.
heads_up: Closed 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. (until 9 a.m. on Sundays and holidays).

name: Penticton Youthpark
why: In Riverside Park at the west end of the beach, with a very large street section of ledges, hubbas, rails, banks, quarter pipes and stair sets alongside a large flow bowl.
heads_up: It's beside a go-kart track and bumper boats, so summer days are busy; public washrooms are nearby and there's a large lot to the north.

name: Penzer Bike Park
why: Part of Penzer Action Park: a BMX-style dirt jump area (2008) and a cement pump track (2017), next to a skatepark, a parkour area and an in-ground trampoline.
heads_up: The pump track is shared with skateboards and scooters, so watch the traffic at busy times.

name: Railside Skate Park
why: At the south end of Lions Park beside the rail yards, mixing a street area of rails, hips, stairs and ledges with a large bowl zone.
heads_up: It sits right beside an active rail yard, so keep clear of the tracks; there's no cover when it rains.

name: Seylynn Bowl
why: A concrete snake run that drops into a bowl, first ridden in 1978 and known as Canada's oldest surviving skatepark. Monty Little, who later designed the original Whistler park, co-designed it.
heads_up: The concrete is decades old with patches and cracks, so walk your line first; it's tucked behind trees by the ball diamonds on Hunter Street, open dawn to dusk.

name: Sicamous Pump Track
why: Asphalt pump track in Finlayson Park that hosted the first UCI Pump Track World Championships Canada Qualifier in 2024, with nearly 50 riders, and the qualifier again in 2025.
heads_up: It sits beside the skatepark and rec centre in Finlayson Park, so it pairs well with a skate session.

name: Sidney Skatepark
why: In Tulista Park about 25 km north of downtown Victoria, pairing a bowl of varied depths with an extension and pocket with a full street section of stairs, a hubba, a handrail, a brick bank and a camel hump.
heads_up: Listed hours are 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.

name: Silver Star Bike Park
why: Lift-served park at Silver Star Mountain Resort above Vernon. When the Georgia Straight covered it in 2013 it had 18 trails over 44 km, including the 7 km Paradise Trail for beginners.
heads_up: Trail figures are from 2013; check the resort for current lift days and tickets.

name: SORCA Bike Skills Park
why: Rebuilt by the Squamish Off-Road Cycling Association next to the Brennan Park Recreation Centre (the original park dates from 2014), with three jump lines (green, blue and double blue), a paved pump track, drops and skinnies.
heads_up: Free to ride; SORCA asks riders to buy an optional yearly trail pass (sold at Corsa Cycles) to pay for upkeep.

name: Squamish BMX Track
why: Refreshed BMX track between Brennan Park and Kinsmen Campground with straights, berm turns, rollers, rhythm sections and tabletops, a short walk from the SORCA skills park.
heads_up: Dirt track: give it time to dry after rain.

name: Stevie Smith Bike Park
why: Velosolutions built a beginner track and a larger competition track here in 2017. The park hosts Red Bull Pump Track World Championship qualifiers, including the only Canadian stop in 2018.
heads_up: The competition track is for confident riders; warm up on the beginner loop.

name: Sun Peaks Bike Park
why: Lift-served park at Sun Peaks Resort near Kamloops, running since 1999, with more than 89 km of trails and 595 m of vertical. It grew onto Sundance Mountain in 2022 and hosts the Canadian National Downhill Championships.
heads_up: Seasonal: the 2026 season ran June 13 to September 27; lift ticket required.

name: Topaz Skatepark
why: A 3,000 m² all-wheels park built by New Line Skateparks that opened in August 2022 in Topaz Park, with a big bowl stepping from 6- and 8-foot pool-block sections to a 10-foot section with steel coping, a street line along the path and smaller beginner features.
heads_up: Floodlights switch off in sequence at 10 p.m. to signal closing; a bike pump track sits next door, so watch for riders.

name: UBC Skatepark
why: Billed as North America's first on-campus concrete skatepark, it packs a bowled mini-ramp, ledges, rails and a ledge shaped like a stack of books into a compact spot on Thunderbird Boulevard.
heads_up: Small footprint, so watch for skaters crossing your line; there's no cover from rain.

name: Vancouver Skate Plaza (Downtown Skateboard Plaza)
why: A 2,000 m² street plaza under the Georgia and Dunsmuir viaducts, opened in 2004 and upgraded in 2011, with replica rails, embankments, curbs, walls and steps in granite, brick, concrete and steel. Complex magazine ranked it #21 on its 2013 list of the world's best skateparks.
heads_up: The viaducts overhead keep most of it dry in the rain, but the city has long planned to remove them and replace the plaza, so check the city page before a trip.

name: Vanier Park Bike Skills Track
why: Built in 2010 and kept up by volunteers, it sits in the trees on the south side of Vanier Park by the Burrard Street Bridge, with dirt jumps of several sizes and two pump tracks, the smaller one for kids.
heads_up: All dirt and no lights: ride in daylight and skip it after heavy rain.

name: Vic West Skatepark
why: Victoria's long-running park at 250 Esquimalt Road, a New Line Skateparks project first built in 2002 with a second phase in 2017, with one fully enclosed bowl, one open flow bowl and modern street terrain.
heads_up: The enclosed bowl has steel and pool coping, so wear a helmet; there's no roof, so let it dry after a shower.

name: Whistler Mountain Bike Park
why: Lift-served park on Whistler Mountain, open since 1999, with over 900 vertical metres of terrain reached by chairlift and gondola. It has hosted Crankworx events, including a pump track challenge at the Boneyard in 2010.
heads_up: Summer lift ticket required; check Whistler Blackcomb for this season's opening and closing dates.

name: Whistler Skatepark
why: Designed by Monty Little and built with Terry Snyder, it opened to skaters in August 1990 with a snake run into a 6.5 m-wide 'Snake Bowl'. Later phases driven by local skaters (the third opened in 2016) grew it past 50,000 sq ft, which the municipality counts as Canada's second-largest skatepark.
heads_up: Open April to November; the lights run until 1 a.m. on a push-button timer, helmets are recommended and mountain bikes aren't allowed. Access is through Day Lot 3.

name: Píhtikwé Skatepark
why: A community-run indoor park whose name is Cree for 'come in'; it opened in Portage Place in fall 2023 and reopened in October 2026 at 323 Portage Avenue, across from Canada Life Centre, with loaner boards, lessons and family sessions.
heads_up: Drop-in sessions run Thursday to Saturday; youth $3, adults $10 and free for Indigenous skaters, and staff will help anyone who can't pay. Check the site for current times.

name: The Plaza at The Forks
why: Opened in 2006 at The Forks, about 44,000 sq ft of plaza with rails, ledges, banks, steps and skateable art such as the steel 'magic carpet', plus an 8,500 sq ft bowl. Designed by van der Zalm + Associates and New Line Skateparks, it was Canada's most expensive skatepark when built ($2.5 million).
heads_up: It's a busy public site, so watch for people walking through the plaza on summer evenings.

name: Garrison Skate Park
why: A 15,300 sq ft 'destination level' park in Fredericton's historic Garrison District, designed and built by New Line Skateparks with local skaters and the city, with plaza terrain, a large enclosed bowl complex and an 'organic flow zone'.
heads_up: Posted rules: one skater in the bowl at a time, and kids under 12 need an adult with them.

name: Moncton Downtown Skate Park
why: Moncton's downtown concrete skatepark, set along Riverfront Park, with a varied layout for skateboarders, scooter riders and freestyle inline skaters of all levels.
heads_up: Free and unsupervised; city rules require a helmet and elbow pads, and it is open until midnight.

name: Station One Skate Plaza
why: A roughly 15,500 sq ft plaza with nautical details beneath the Route 1 overpass beside Harbour Passage, built as a downtown hub for youth in New Line Skateparks' portfolio.
heads_up: Free and well lit, with the overpass overhead; bring a helmet.

name: Kenmount Terrace Skate Park
why: A newer street park on Messenger Drive, designed with local skaters, the city and skatepark designers, with a steep cantilevered bank, a bank-to-pole jam, a wedge ramp with rooftop ledge, slappy banks and a 3-stair with manual pad.
heads_up: Wear a helmet and pads, as the city asks.

name: Northwest Rotary Skate Park (Mundy Pond)
why: A 16,600 sq ft concrete park in Mundy Pond Park, built in 2004–05 as the province's first professionally planned skatepark, with a 3-ft bowl that rolls into a 6–8 ft bowl with extensions, escalators and hips, plus banks, hubbas, stairs and gaps.
heads_up: Wear a helmet and pads, as the city asks; it is a big bowl, so read the lines before dropping in.

name: Team Gushue Skatepark
why: A New Line Skateparks redesign-build at the Team Gushue Sports Complex, with stair sets and bank ramps dropping into a lower plaza and two horseshoe mini-ramp sections joined by a spine.
heads_up: Stair sets and banks drop into the lower plaza, so check your landings before you roll in.

name: Bridgewater Skate Park
why: A 10,000 sq ft permanent concrete park on York Street on the South Shore, with a concrete bowl and street obstacles, built through a community fundraising campaign (estimated cost $645,000).
heads_up: Helmets are not required inside the park, but the law requires one on the streets you ride to get there.

name: Dartmouth Commons Skatepark
why: Designed and built by Grindline with local firm Ocean Contractors on the Dartmouth Common across from the Sportsplex, this Pacific Northwest-style concrete park opened in June 2016 after a push by local skaters that went back decades.
heads_up: The Halifax Common skatepark across the harbour closed in June 2026 for a full rebuild (up to a year), so plan on this one for now.

name: Ashbridges Bay Skatepark (Beach Skatepark)
why: Toronto's largest skatepark, beside Woodbine Beach: a street plaza designed by Spectrum Skateparks (about 21,500 sq ft of concrete, with a floating manual dish and a kinked bank) plus an 11-ft kidney bowl with pool coping.
heads_up: No washrooms on site, and the bowl is deep: leave it to experienced skaters and take turns.

name: Bayview Arena Bike Park
why: A 3,000 m² dirt park behind Bayview Arena in North York with jumps, berms and tabletops for a range of skill levels.
heads_up: Open dawn to dusk; park at the arena. Let the dirt dry after rain.

name: Carlington Bike Park
why: Led by the Ottawa Mountain Bike Association with the City of Ottawa, it sits on the former ski hill in Carlington Park, with three granite-surface circuits for beginner to advanced riders.
heads_up: Easy to reach by bus and bike path, so you don't need a car.

name: Centennial Park Pan Am BMX Centre
why: The BMX venue of the Toronto 2015 Pan Am Games: a compact closed-loop course with four straights, three banked turns, 5 m and 8 m start ramps and several challenging jumps.
heads_up: Open dawn to dusk from May 2 to October 31, weather permitting.

name: Charlie Bowins Skatepark (McNabb Park)
why: Downtown Ottawa's central skatepark in McNabb Park on Bronson Ave, built in 2015 and named for local pro Charlie Bowins, who led the push for it; skaters raised $25,000 of its $100,000 cost.
heads_up: A smaller community park, so expect to share lines; trees give shade on hot days.

name: CJ's Skatepark
why: A year-round indoor skatepark in Mississauga that runs two-hour sessions, vert sessions, a Friday girls' session, lessons, camps and a pro shop.
heads_up: Sessions run in two-hour blocks and hours change in winter and summer; call 905-272-6888 to confirm.

name: Dunbat Skatepark (Alexandra Park)
why: A small downtown park in Alexandra Park at Dundas and Bathurst with ledges, manual pads, banks and a 5-ft mini ramp, known for a laid-back session and manual pads that get rotated each year.
heads_up: Open spring to fall with lights until 11 pm; washrooms are at Scadding Court Community Centre.

name: East York Skatepark
why: Opened in 2007 by Stan Wadlow Park, it pairs a street plaza (stair sets, handrails, hubbas, a flat gap) with a tight 5-ft figure-eight bowl with a hip and roll-in, and is very popular with Toronto skaters.
heads_up: Washrooms are at the Stan Wadlow Clubhouse; the bowl is tight, so watch a few runs before dropping in.

name: Eighth Street Skatepark (Jordon Carter Memorial Park)
why: A 13,000 sq ft New Line park in New Toronto (Etobicoke) that mixes a 5-ft peanut bowl, quarter pipes with hips and a vert wall with hubbas, a taco bank, stairs and handrails.
heads_up: No washrooms on site; open 8 am to 11 pm.

name: Jimmie Simpson Recreation Centre indoor skatepark
why: A City of Toronto indoor drop-in for ages 13 to 24, with wooden and prefab ramps, rails and ledges set up on a gym floor through fall, winter and spring.
heads_up: Ages 13 to 24 only, at city drop-in times; call 416-392-0751 before you go.

name: Joyride 150
why: Indoor bike park that opened in December 2009 in a building of over 100,000 sq ft, with beginner to expert sections, a foam pit and resi jump, jump and rhythm lines, a BMX street park, a pump track and an indoor cross-country loop.
heads_up: Paid day passes (about $31 for ages 7 and up, less after 7 p.m.); bring your own bike and helmet or rent them there.

name: Kivi Park Pump Track
why: A newer intermediate dirt pump track with banked turns and rollers at Kivi Park, which has more than 55 km of trails.
heads_up: Kivi Park charges a day pass ($9, family $25, kids 10 and under free); bike rentals from $25 for 2 hours.

name: Kiwanis Skateboard Plaza
why: A plaza of about 1,700 m² with hubba ledges, C-ledges, banks, a coin bank, a jersey barrier, a transition gap, a 6-stair rail and a replica of the Pier 7 manual pads.
heads_up: No lights, and London parks close from 10 pm to 6 am.

name: Legacy Skatepark
why: Built by Spectrum Skateparks for the City of Ottawa and opened in October 2004, the 18,300 sq ft Nepean park is Ottawa's largest, with an open-ended bowl with a spine, a big central funbox, hubbas, rails, stairs and manual pads; it has hosted Wild in the Parks and Go Skateboarding Day.
heads_up: Free and unsupervised, with no pads required; it sits behind the Centrepoint Theatres, which have a large parking lot.

name: Medway-Kiwanis Skate Bowls
why: London's transition park: bowls with a wave, roll-in, near-vert wall ride, clamshell, waterfalls, corners and multiple hips, a 56-degree 'mullet', and a pump track.
heads_up: No lights (London does not light its skate parks), and city parks close from 10 pm to 6 am.

name: Phil Esposito Park Pump Track
why: One of the first asphalt pump tracks in Ontario, with beginner rollers and banked turns plus an advanced 'butterfly' route, linked to more than 30 km of mountain bike trails.
heads_up: Bike rentals are available in town for about $50 a day.

name: Prince Arthur's Landing Skateboard & BMX Plaza
why: A nearly 25,000 sq ft skate and BMX plaza in Marina Park on the Lake Superior waterfront, with a skateable re-creation of the Sleeping Giant, ledges and walls of local stone, and a classic-style pool bowl.
heads_up: Open daily 6 am to 11 pm and shared with BMX riders.

name: Sunnyside Bike Park
why: Opened in 2014 about 150 m from Lake Ontario, partly from recycled materials, with pump tracks, a skills trail, a large drop, a boardwalk and a wall ride, rated green to black.
heads_up: Open dawn to dusk; no parking on site, only a drop-off roundabout at Lake Shore Blvd. W. and Ellis Ave.

name: Underpass Park Skatepark
why: Part of Underpass Park in the West Don Lands, opened in 2012 beneath the Adelaide, Eastern and Richmond overpasses; the roadway overhead gives the skate area shelter from rain and snow.
heads_up: Smaller modular obstacles and no washrooms on site; covered, but not enclosed.

name: Vanderhoof Skatepark
why: Known locally as "the Hoof", it is built around a big U-shaped bowl with a 9-ft deep end and pool coping that many skaters rate the best bowl in Ontario; a small street area sits alongside.
heads_up: No washrooms and only a basic street section, so come for the bowl; street parking on Vanderhoof Ave and Research Rd.

name: Waterdown Memorial Park Skatepark
why: A New Line concrete park in Waterdown Memorial Park known for a smooth bowl with plenty of lines, a clamshell, spine, roll-in and hips, plus a flat bar, ledges and curbs.
heads_up: Mostly transition, with few street lines; free parking in the adjacent lot.

name: Wolseley Skatepark
why: An all-levels London park with a replica pool, rollers, a 9-stair with rails, flat and double stair sets, floating kickers and a 30-brick euro hip.
heads_up: No lights, and London parks close from 10 pm to 6 am.

name: Charlottetown Skate Park (Victoria Park)
why: PEI's capital-city park: about 10,000 sq ft of concrete and polyboard ramps behind Memorial Ballfield in Victoria Park, designed with input from local skaters.
heads_up: Helmets are required; open 8 am to 11 pm and closed in bad weather.

name: Adrénaline Urbaine
why: A year-round action-sports centre in Trois-Rivières with an indoor skatepark and an outdoor one, alongside a bouldering wall, a ninja course and a four-season ski slope on the roof.
heads_up: Rates and hours are posted on adrenalineurbaine.ca; free parking.

name: Camp Fortune Pump Track
why: Camp Fortune's pump track sits on NCC land in Gatineau Park. A 2023 federal assessment covered a 215 m expansion with a start ramp, two berms, five tabletops and six rollers, the first phase of a mountain bike skills park.
heads_up: It is built on native soil, so wait for it to dry after rain.

name: Empire 47 Pump Track
why: At 1,800 m² it is the largest pump track in the Quebec City area. The Velosolutions-built track has hosted a Red Bull UCI Pump Track World Championships qualifier and is lit in the evening.
heads_up: Paid access (adult day pass about $24), and the park closes on rainy days.

name: Le TAZ
why: The City of Montréal calls Le TAZ Canada's largest indoor skatepark: a year-round centre in the Saint-Michel environmental complex with ramps, bowls, rails and street features for skaters, inline skaters, BMX and scooter riders from beginner to pro.
heads_up: Minimum age 6; buy tickets on site or through Loisirs Montréal, and check taz.ca for session times.

name: Parc Ahuntsic Skatepark
why: A $2.3-million, 1,800 m² reinforced-concrete street course that opened in late 2022, with three levels of mini ramps, hips, corner pockets, a long pyramid with rail and ledge, manual pads and a volcano.
heads_up: Boards, scooters and pads can be borrowed free from the Hélène-Charbonneau Library across the street; free Saturday intro sessions in summer.

name: Parc Delorme Skatepark
why: A 1,250 m² concrete plaza in Saint-Léonard opened in 2020 with 26 elements over 2.5 m of elevation change, mixing street and transition sections, and one of the few Montreal parks built for skateboards, inline skates, scooters and BMX alike.
heads_up: Closed in rain, frost or snow and unsupervised; kids under 12 need an adult. Trees give shade by day and lights come on at night.

name: Parc du Père-Marquette Skatepark
why: A 1,300 m² skate plaza in Rosemont–La Petite-Patrie opened in 2018 and shaped by a skater committee that gathered more than 800 suggestions; it has a bank-to-wall, china bank, ledges, rails, a corner-bowl mini ramp and a 'sushi dipping bowl'.
heads_up: Open mid-April to mid-November; lights run until 11 pm, but it closes at 8:30 pm Thursday to Sunday.

name: Parc Honoré-Mercier Skatepark
why: A $2-million concrete skatepark in Mercier–Hochelaga-Maisonneuve that opened in 2022 after planning from 2019 with residents, neighbourhood groups and the Association Skateboard Montréal, with concrete modules, a scooter track and a misting system for hot days.
heads_up: Shared with scooter riders, with play areas for small kids right beside it.

name: Parc Jarry Skatepark
why: A free concrete skatepark in Parc Jarry, off Rue Jarry Ouest beside the parking lot and basketball courts, with a five-section course for technical and freestyle skating.
heads_up: Open 6 am to 11 pm; helmet and pads recommended, and riding on the roads, sidewalks and squares around it is prohibited.

name: Parc Victoria Skatepark
why: A $1.1-million skatepark in Parc Victoria in Saint-Roch, opened in June 2011 after users were consulted, lit for evening sessions and built for skateboarders and roller skaters, with a BMX area alongside.
heads_up: Open daily 7 am to 11 pm from May to October only; helmet and pads strongly recommended.

name: Peace Park (Place de la Paix)
why: A granite square on Saint-Laurent Blvd, designed by Robert Desjardins and opened in 1994, whose long ledges and stairs made it Montreal's best-known street spot; after years of tickets the city legalized skating there in 2015.
heads_up: Skating is legal, but it is a busy public square in front of the Monument-National: give pedestrians room.

name: Pointe-Claire Skatepark
why: A 12,000 sq ft West Island park with a bowl, a capsule, a mini ramp and a wave, suited to beginners and experienced riders alike.
heads_up: Helmets are required here.

name: SPIN Skatepark
why: An indoor skatepark and skate shop in Brossard on Montreal's South Shore, open year-round with lessons, summer camps, sales and service, and equipment rental; the same team built Brossard's outdoor planchodrome, which opened in May 2020.
heads_up: Check spinskatepark.com or call 450-890-9520 for session times before you go.

name: The Big O pipe
why: A concrete full pipe that spills into a halfpipe at the Olympic Stadium, skated since the 1980s; to save it from the Saputo Stadium expansion the pipe was moved about 25 m, reopening in August 2013.
heads_up: There is no deck at the top and slams land on flat: not a place to learn transition.

name: Van Horne Skatepark (Skatepark du Mile-End)
why: Opened in 2019 under the Van Horne overpass in Mile End; when it was planned it was the largest street-style park in Quebec, and a snake run links its bowl section to long parallel street lines.
heads_up: The overpass covers part of the park, so some lines stay dry in light rain; about five minutes' walk from Rosemont metro.

name: Vans Skatepark (Olympic Park)
why: Built by California Skateparks with Vans on the Olympic Stadium esplanade: a 900 m² pro bowl that opened with a Vans Park Series contest in July 2019, plus a 10,000 m² street section added on Go Skateboarding Day 2021.
heads_up: Free, open 9 am to 9 pm; there is no shade on the esplanade, so bring sunscreen and water.

name: Verdun Skatepark (Parc Arthur-Therrien)
why: A riverside street park in Verdun designed by Dan Vézina as a 'mini-city' after the 1980s Atari game 720°, with curbs, streetlamps and crosswalk markings; a 24 m by 18 m bowl was added in 2021.
heads_up: Open 7 am to 10 pm with evening lights, drinking water and washrooms; next to Verdun's urban beach.

name: Parque de la Amistad Skatepark
why: A street-and-transition park inside Parque de la Amistad on Circuito Otay Lago in east Tijuana.
heads_up: It is inside a city park, so check the park's opening hours before you go.

name: Skatepark Río Nuevo
why: A street-and-bowl park on Calle Álamo in Mexicali.
heads_up: Mexicali summers are extremely hot, so skate early or after sunset and bring water.

name: Bowls de Pescadero
why: A set of bowls at km 64 of Highway 19 in Barrio Las Palmitas, El Pescadero, the surf town south of Todos Santos.
heads_up: It is out on the highway, so check conditions locally before you drive out.

name: Skatepark 5 de Febrero
why: A street-and-transition park on the Carretera Transpeninsular in the 5 de Febrero neighbourhood of San José del Cabo.
heads_up: It is right by the highway, so watch traffic getting in and out and bring water.

name: Skatepark Atardeceres
why: A street-and-bowl park on Calzada El Camino Real in La Paz.
heads_up: The sun is strong year-round in La Paz, so bring water and shade breaks.

name: La Duna Skatepark
why: A pink-concrete park in Parque Oriente whose forms were inspired by the Samalayuca dunes, built around 2021 under a federal urban improvement programme with separate bowl, street and beginner zones, classrooms and a viewing deck.
heads_up: The trees planted for shade were still young when it opened, so the desert sun hits hard; go early or late.

name: Skatepark Sacramento
why: A 3,500 m² concrete street park in Quintas Carolinas with hubbas, rails, a Pappalardo ledge, a gap nicknamed the Chinga Gap, slappy curbs, quarter pipes and a mini ramp.
heads_up: Mostly street terrain; the mini ramp is the only real transition.

name: Bowls de Cabeza de Juárez
why: A circuit of concrete bowls inside the Unidad Deportiva Iztapalapa at Cabeza de Juárez; it has been there for many years and Récord called it one of the most emblematic skate spots in Mexico.
heads_up: The concrete is old and not all of it is in good shape, so check the surface before committing; entry is free.

name: La Mexicana Skatepark
why: California Skateparks designed and built this 25,000 sq ft park in Parque La Mexicana in Santa Fe, with a large flow bowl, a volcano, hubba ledges, stair sets and manual pads.
heads_up: Listed hours are 8am to 8pm; the bowl has steel coping and varied depths, so check the deep end before you drop in.

name: Nike Templo Mayor Skatepark
why: Built by California Skateparks with Nike SB and the city government in Parque de la Juventud, it was the first certified Street League plaza outside the United States; the colour work and hubba designs are by artist Luis Ponce.
heads_up: The hubbas and stair sets are contest-sized; newer skaters will get more out of the banks and flat ledges.

name: San Cosme Skatepark (El Mara)
why: Built under the Circuito Interior overpass at Ribera de San Cosme on the site of an old minibus stop, it draws hundreds of skaters and riders and got a 2019 makeover with art by Dago and David No Existe.
heads_up: Entry is free, whatever anyone tells you; the overpass gives shade and some cover from rain.

name: Skatepark Azcapotzalco "Capital Joven"
why: A Street League-certified street plaza inside Deportivo Reynosa, designed and built by California Skateparks with a circuit layout so lines flow without collisions.
heads_up: It is inside a sports complex with listed hours of about 9am to 6pm, so plan on daytime sessions.

name: Skatepark Bosque de San Juan de Aragón
why: Roughly 7,000 m² of concrete in the Bosque de San Juan de Aragón, with two big flow bowls with mellow transitions plus ledges, stairs, rails and manual pads, used by skaters, rollers and BMX riders.
heads_up: Listed hours are 6am to 6pm; the nearest Metro stop is Bosque de Aragón.

name: Skatepark Constituyentes
why: A 4,223 m² concrete park in the second section of Bosque de Chapultepec, opened as part of the section's 2016 renovation, with two flow bowls, stair sets, ledges, rails and mini ramps.
heads_up: Time Out lists daily hours of 7am to 7pm and board rental on site; the nearest Metro stop is Constituyentes.

name: Skatepark Los Coyotes
why: Laid out in the shape of an axolotl's head in the green area of Parque Los Coyotes in Coapa, opened in 2017 with a rainwater capture system, and fitted with boxes, rails, quarters and funboxes.
heads_up: Shared with BMX riders; kiosks on site sell snacks and drinks.

name: Skatepark Olímpico Cuitláhuac
why: In Iztapalapa's Parque Cuitláhuac, a park built on a former landfill, with eight ramps, 12 street obstacles and an Olympic-style bowl; it was renovated in 2021.
heads_up: It is in the far east of the city inside a large park that also has a baseball field and go-kart track; plan your trip and go in daylight.

name: Bowl de Valle de Bravo
why: A concrete bowl in Santa María Ahuacatlán, Valle de Bravo, the lakeside town west of Toluca.
heads_up: Summer afternoons often bring rain in the highlands, so morning sessions are the safest bet.

name: Parque Extremo
why: A street-and-bowl park on Blvd. Epsilon in León's Valle de Las Haciendas area, mapped as a dedicated skateboard sports centre.
heads_up: It is on León's southeast side, so plan transport.

name: Troncones Skatepark (Tres Santos)
why: A street-and-bowl park on the main road of Playa Troncones, the surf village north of Zihuatanejo.
heads_up: Coastal humidity and rain can leave the concrete slick, so check it before you skate.

name: La Plutarco Skatepark (Mamatore)
why: A street-and-transition park on Av. 4 in Pachuca's Plutarco Elías Calles neighbourhood.
heads_up: Pachuca is windy, so expect gusts on the higher features.

name: El Frijol DIY
why: A local DIY built by and for skaters over a basketball court in Lomas de Zapopan, also called La Lechera or Parque de Los Duendes; its pool-style Bean Bowl has concrete pool coping and sections over 7 feet deep.
heads_up: The bowl is tight and tricky, so watch the locals' lines first and help keep the spot clean.

name: El Pípila Skatepark
why: Its bowl hosted the 2015 Pipila Bowl Skate Jam, which drew 43 skaters from across Mexico and was one of the first bowl contests in Jalisco since the 1970s parks closed.
heads_up: It is at Av. Constitución and Vallarta Oriente in Tlajomulco, on the far south side of the Guadalajara metro area.

name: La Curva Skatepark
why: A city-backed park on Blvd. Panamericano in Zapopan, opened around 2022, with street features and a mid-size bowl that has an over-vert capsule.
heads_up: It is next door to Zapopan's public safety building; the over-vert section is for experienced skaters.

name: Skatepark Ajijic (El Charal)
why: A concrete bowl on the Ajijic malecón by Lake Chapala, which Mexico News Daily described in 2020 as in excellent condition.
heads_up: It is mapped as lit, so evening sessions are possible.

name: Skatepark Montenegro
why: A very large park on the Chapala highway at the south edge of metro Guadalajara, with several bowls, odd transitions and transfer lines; it hosted a Vans BMX Pro Cup stop in 2017 and a Santa Cruz skate team demo in 2026.
heads_up: Shared with BMX riders, and it is a long way from central Guadalajara, so plan transport.

name: Skatepark Bosque Cuauhtémoc
why: A street-and-transition park in Bosque Cuauhtémoc, on the edge of Morelia's historic centre; locals call it Bosquerrics.
heads_up: It sits in a public park used by walkers and families, so keep lines clear of the paths.

name: Venus Skatepark
why: A municipal street-and-bowl park on Av. 50 Metros in Jiutepec, next to Cuernavaca, run by the Ayuntamiento de Jiutepec and opened in July 2022.
heads_up: Free and lit, according to its OpenStreetMap record.

name: Shore Skatepark
why: Dreamland Skateparks lists this concrete park on the Punta de Mita road as a DIY collaboration with Shore; it has a bowl, a spine and quarter pipes, banks, a mini ramp, pyramids and ledges.
heads_up: It is on the highway beside Rancho Dora near La Cruz de Huanacaxtle; access terms are not published, so check before you go.

name: San Miguel Skatepark
why: A street-and-bowl park on Loma Larga in Lomas de San Miguel, Guadalupe, on the east side of metro Monterrey.
heads_up: Monterrey summers are very hot, so plan morning or evening sessions.

name: Skatepark Las Palmas
why: A street park in La Crucecita, the town centre of Huatulco on the Oaxaca coast.
heads_up: The coastal sun is strong, so bring water.

name: Alcanfores Skatepark
why: A street-and-bowl park on Jesús Romero Flores in the Constituyentes Fovissste neighbourhood of Querétaro city.
heads_up: A neighbourhood park; check the bowl for standing water after rain.

name: Skatepark DIF Playa del Carmen
why: A street-and-bowl park on Calle 8 Norte in central Playa del Carmen.
heads_up: Tropical downpours leave standing water on the concrete; give it time to dry before you skate.

name: Skatepark Kilómetro 0
why: A street-and-bowl park at Av. Reforma and Justo Sierra, beside Mazatlán's baseball stadium.
heads_up: Mazatlán is hot and humid much of the year, so bring water.

name: El Bowl Parque La Ruina
why: A concrete bowl built by California Skateparks in Parque La Ruina in central Hermosillo.
heads_up: Hermosillo summers are extremely hot, so skate in the morning or evening and bring water.

name: Skatepark Bicentenario Xalapa
why: A street-and-bowl park in Xalapa's Zona Centro, close to downtown.
heads_up: Xalapa is wet and misty much of the year, so check the ground before you head out.

name: Auburn/Opelika Skate Park
why: A pour-in-place concrete park built by American Ramp Company as a joint project of the cities of Auburn and Opelika at Pines Crossing Golf Course, opened in January 2020 with a large bowl as its centrepiece.
heads_up: At Pines Crossing Golf Course; check Auburn Parks and Recreation for hours.

name: CityWalk BHAM Skatepark
why: The skatepark at CityWalk BHAM, the public space built beneath the elevated I-59/I-20 corridor downtown, with several bowls, a snake run, a street plaza and a flow course.
heads_up: Hours run roughly 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. and change with the season.

name: Skate Depot
why: The City of Cullman's 8,000-square-foot Spohn Ranch park on Second Avenue NE by Depot Park, opened in November 2022 with ramps, a drop-in bowl, rails and wedges.
heads_up: Open to skateboards, rollerblades, BMX and scooters, so keep an eye out for bikes.

name: Taku Skatepark
why: Rebuilt by Grindline in 2024, Taku is Anchorage's largest skatepark, mixing flow and plaza terrain with a whale tail-shaped bowl and a Big Dipper inlay, paid for by donations, voter-approved bonds and a Skatepark Project grant.
heads_up: Outdoor and snowbound in winter, so plan on late spring to early fall.

name: Bushmaster Skate Park
why: Designed by SITE Design Group and opened in 1998, this 13,000 sq ft park won an Editor's Choice award for best new public park and a 10 out of 10 from Thrasher; it has a clover bowl of several depths and a snake run.
heads_up: No lights, no supervision and no gear rules; skate it in daylight, and expect snow to shut it in a Flagstaff winter.

name: Cesar Chavez Skate Plaza
why: A lit street plaza in Laveen laid out in the shape of the letter A, with nearly 10,000 sq ft of five intersecting paths, a four-stair with a rail, steel and concrete ledges and a gap over a gravel pit.
heads_up: Street only, no bowls; lights make it the go-to after the heat breaks.

name: Desert West Skate Park
why: A 25,000 sq ft Maryvale park with three bowls from 5 to 13 feet deep beside a street area of curbs, steps with steel ledges, hips and banks; it hosts Cowtown Skateboards' annual PHX AM contest.
heads_up: Desert sun on bare concrete: midsummer afternoons are too hot, so go early or at night.

name: El Mirage Skatepark
why: A roughly 15,000 sq ft California Skateparks plaza in the West Valley with hubba ledges, flat ledges, kinked rails, a stair set, manual pads, big flat banks and quarter pipes.
heads_up: Listed as open 24/7; bring water and avoid summer middays.

name: Foxglenn Skatepark
why: A 16,000 sq ft SITE Design park from 2002, mostly transition with bowls, extensions and hips, quarter pipes and bank ramps, plus a tall down ledge, flat ledges and rails.
heads_up: Open 6 a.m. to 9 p.m.; crowded on weekends.

name: Goodyear Skate Park
why: A roughly 32,000 sq ft California Skateparks build west of Phoenix with a full-pipe capsule, a snake run and a peanut bowl with pool coping next to a street section of hubbas, banks and a pyramid.
heads_up: About 30 minutes from downtown Phoenix; summer heat means early mornings or evenings.

name: Jack Malmgren Skate Park
why: At Posse Grounds Park, this park pairs a bowl with shallow and deep ends and a flow area with vert and a volcano with a street section, all against Sedona's red-rock backdrop.
heads_up: No lights, so plan a daytime session, and bring water: the high-desert sun is strong.

name: Paradise Valley Skate Park
why: One of Phoenix's largest and longest-running parks: about 26,000 sq ft by SITE Design Group with kinked snake bowls, spine bowls into a square bowl, a kidney bowl, a banked alley and a street plaza with flat bars, ledges and blocks.
heads_up: Phoenix heat is serious from May to September; skate early or under the lights in the evening and bring water.

name: Pecos Park Skate Park
why: At about 29,500 sq ft this SITE Design Group park in Ahwatukee is one of Phoenix's largest, with a street plaza of flat bars, ledges and blocks, pump bumps, sloped ramps and bowls.
heads_up: Bring water in summer and skate early or late, when the concrete has cooled.

name: The Deck Skatepark (Eastmark)
why: Spohn Ranch built this 20,000 sq ft park in Mesa's Eastmark neighborhood in 2022, a large street plaza with transition elements and a concrete pump track.
heads_up: Desert heat: skip the midday hours from May to September and bring water.

name: The Wedge Skatepark (Eldorado Park)
why: About 20,000 sq ft in Eldorado Park with an amoeba bowl, quarter pipes, pyramids, curbs, rails and plenty of flat ground; the spread-out, fairly mellow layout makes it a good place to learn.
heads_up: Good first stop for new skaters; summer afternoons are too hot, so go early or late.

name: Kanis Skatepark
why: A deep late-1980s peanut bowl, a DIY zone built by the Kanis DIY Krew over about 15 years, and a 2016 Hunger Skateparks addition with corner pockets, hips, a spine and a steep bank wall; the Kanis Bash draws skaters every year around Halloween.
heads_up: The old bowl is deep and steep; watch a few runs before you drop in.

name: Riverfront Skate and Bike Park
why: A city-owned skate and bike park on Riverfront Drive in downtown Fort Smith, opened in 2018, with a skate park of about 14,500 square feet built by American Ramp Company plus an asphalt pump track and bike skills lines.
heads_up: Skate park, pump track and bike lines sit side by side, so watch for riders crossing between them.

name: Runway Bike Park
why: Velosolutions designed the asphalt pump track at The Jones Center: about 25,000 sq ft. It opened in fall 2018 and that October hosted the first Red Bull Pump Track World Championship final. The 2.75-acre park also has three asphalt skills lines with cedar and steel features, and a bicycle playground for small kids.
heads_up: The Jones Center lends out bikes and helmets for free, so you can ride without bringing your own.

name: Alga Norte Skatepark
why: Built by Stantec in 2014 in Alga Norte Community Park, it pairs a three-lobed combi bowl and a square bowl with a street plaza whose big quarterpipe has a lip shaped after the area's Spanish-mission style.
heads_up: Open 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

name: Beach Park Skatepark
why: Bakersfield's oldest concrete skatepark, opened in 2008 along the Kern River, has a large street plaza and a concrete bowl, with lights added in 2019 for night sessions.
heads_up: Open dawn to 9 p.m.; summer evenings under the lights beat the afternoon heat.

name: Belvedere Skatepark
why: A $1.1 million park in East LA built by Lawrence R. Moss & Associates, with pools, a wall ride and vert waves; Tony Alva was among the local pros who tested the concrete when it opened.
heads_up: Mostly pool and transition terrain, so pads are a good idea.

name: Channel Street Skatepark
why: Volunteers began building this DIY under the 110 Freeway at Channel and Gaffey streets in San Pedro in the early 2000s; freeway work closed it in 2014 and the San Pedro Skatepark Association reopened it legally in August 2022.
heads_up: Volunteer-run DIY with rough, tight transitions; respect the locals and the rules posted by the association.

name: Chicano Park Skatepark
why: Skaters built this street-style DIY under the Coronado Bridge in Barrio Logan's Chicano Park, among its famous murals, with long quarterpipes, an A-frame rail and a car-shaped box.
heads_up: DIY flat ground with cracks that catch wheels; open dawn to dusk, no lights.

name: Culver City Skatepark
why: Created by the city with a group of local skaters, it mixes ledges, rails and a flow area with a clover-shaped pool often named among the best skatepark pools in Southern California.
heads_up: Lessons and classes run here at set times; check the city schedule if you want an open session.

name: Derby Park Skatepark
why: One of the first public skateparks in the world, built in the 1970s to Ken Wormhoudt's design, Derby's snake run and bowl were resurfaced in 2012 with his son Zach consulting.
heads_up: Old-school concrete with short, tight lines; an expansion next to the snake run has been under city review.

name: Encinitas Skatepark (Poods)
why: Known as Poods, this Cardiff park is a multi-tier street plaza of big banks, ledges, stairs and hubbas, with a three-lobed backyard-style bowl trimmed in pool coping.
heads_up: Open 8 a.m. to sunset; the surface is slippery, especially on hard wheels.

name: Etnies Skatepark of Lake Forest
why: Opened December 13, 2003 as a joint venture of the city and etnies and designed by SITE Design Group, it grew past 62,000 sq ft with a 2011 expansion and is described as California's largest free skatepark.
heads_up: Entry needs a park ID card: free for Lake Forest and Foothill Ranch residents, a one-time $15 for everyone else.

name: Hemet Skatepark (Gibbel Skate Plaza)
why: Opened in 2023 and designed by Kanten Russell of New Line Skateparks, the Riverside County park has a vert bowl with a square shallow end, a flow bowl and a big street plaza that echoes his Poods design.
heads_up: Fenced, open 6 a.m. to dusk; summer afternoons get very hot, so go early.

name: Humboldt Neighborhood Skate Park
why: Grindline remodeled Chico's Humboldt Avenue park in 2018 with fresh concrete and a new bowl that Tony Hawk skated and used as the model for a bowl at his Wilmington, North Carolina park.
heads_up: Bowl-focused, so bring pads if you're new to transition.

name: Ken Wormhoudt Skate Park (Mike Fox Park)
why: Designed by Wormhoudt Inc. beside the San Lorenzo River, the 15,000 sq ft city park has a full pipe, two bowls with pool coping and tile, a practice bowl and a street course with steps, hubbas and rails.
heads_up: Helmet, elbow and knee pads are required, and the park closes when wet; open 9 a.m. to sunset.

name: Lake Cunningham Regional Skate Park
why: San Jose's 68,000 sq ft park at Lake Cunningham has a 22-foot-tall full pipe, 10 bowls ranging from beginner to expert and a street course.
heads_up: Small entry fee or annual pass; closes about 30 minutes before sunset.

name: Linda Vista Skatepark
why: San Diego's flagship city park opened January 16, 2018 after skaters, pros and neighbors shaped the design, with several bowls, a full pipe, a street course and a bridge for watching.
heads_up: Lit and open 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. daily; shade structures help on hot days.

name: Magdalena Ecke Family YMCA Skate Park
why: An all-concrete YMCA park with a 10-foot vert half-pipe donated by Olympian Bryce Wettstein, a kidney pool for experienced skaters, plaza elements, mini ramps and a beginner area called Mini Land.
heads_up: $12 session or membership, no cash; helmets for everyone and pads under 18; weekday sessions start at 3 p.m.

name: McClatchy Park Skatepark
why: Spohn Ranch built this 7,000 sq ft concrete park in Sacramento's McClatchy Park in 2014; it is unsupervised and open to the public for skateboarding and inline skating.
heads_up: Sacramento city code requires helmet, elbow pads and knee pads at every city skatepark, and riders can be cited.

name: Memorial Skatepark (Bill and Maxine Wilson Skatepark)
why: Opened in 2004 next to the Memorial Recreation Center, the 22,000 sq ft park has a 10-foot keyhole bowl with pool coping, a 90-foot snake run, a butterfly-shaped mini bowl and a big sunken street plaza.
heads_up: Fenced, open 10 a.m. to dusk, no lights.

name: Mission Valley YMCA Krause Family Skate & Bike Park
why: The 60,000 sq ft YMCA park in Clairemont has a Dew Tour vert ramp, a concrete pool, a mini ramp with a spine, a street course and the first permanent skatercross track, designed by Andy Macdonald.
heads_up: YMCA-run with passes or memberships and helmets required; check open-skate hours before you go.

name: Pacifica Skatepark
why: Next to Pacifica State Beach, the 14,000 sq ft concrete park opened in 2005 after a skater-led campaign that began in 1998, with Tony Hawk consulted on the design; it has a large pool, three bowls and rails.
heads_up: Right by the ocean, so sea mist can leave the concrete damp on grey days.

name: Pedlow Field Skatepark
why: The first public skatepark in Los Angeles when it opened in Encino on February 17, 2001, it reopened with new features in 2006 and has a large pool, a snake run bowl, a pyramid and rails.
heads_up: No lights, so sessions end at dusk.

name: Pier 7
why: A classic San Francisco street spot on the Embarcadero waterfront, Pier 7 was skate-stopped for years until skaters removed the wooden slats and metal stoppers and restored its concrete pads in summer 2021; the Port has let skating continue.
heads_up: Not a skatepark: it's a public pier plaza, so yield to walkers, and stoppers could return.

name: Potrero del Sol Skatepark
why: Designed by Dreamland and built by Grindline, San Francisco's largest skatepark opened July 2, 2008 in the Mission's La Raza Park, with a street course, pool blocks, a deep end and a quarterpipe around the edge.
heads_up: Busy with Mission locals; take turns and watch the lines in the deep end.

name: Prince Memorial Skatepark (Alex Road)
why: Designed by Grindline and built by California Skateparks, the former Alex Road park has a combi bowl, a tiled backyard-style pool and two snake runs, one ending in an over-vert capsule, plus a small street section.
heads_up: Next to Oceanside's airport, three miles from downtown; locals report no running water, so bring your own.

name: Provident Skate Park
why: A community drive led by the Kaweah Delta Health Care District from 1996 raised over $260,000 for this Recreation Park skatepark, designed with local skaters, with a big funbox, volcanoes and a snake run that ends in a bowl.
heads_up: Central Valley summers are hot, so skate early or late.

name: Robb Field Skatepark
why: Opened in February 2000 as the first skatepark built and run by the City of San Diego, its 40,000 sq ft street course at the entrance to Ocean Beach has a combination bowl, handrails, ledges, a pump bump and an octagon volcano.
heads_up: Open 10 a.m. to dusk every day, including holidays.

name: San Clemente Skatepark
why: The 14,000 sq ft park in Richard T. Steed Memorial Sports Park, also called Ralphs, has three mini ramps with bowl corners, a mellow flow bowl and street features, and it is where Ryan Sheckler came up.
heads_up: Small for the crowd it draws, so expect lines; dawn to dusk, no lights.

name: Skater's Point
why: Santa Barbara's 14,600 sq ft city skatepark sits on the waterfront along Cabrillo Boulevard east of Stearns Wharf, next to the beach bike path; local painters refreshed its walls in 2023.
heads_up: Beachfront and unlit, so it's a daytime session.

name: Skatin' Place, Golden Gate Park
why: A long-standing roller skating spot on the JFK Promenade near 6th Avenue, now marked by a 28-by-93-foot ground mural honoring the park's skating history, painted by Aimee Stevland with input from Church of 8 Wheels founder David Miles Jr.
heads_up: Flat asphalt for quad and inline sessions, not ramps; Golden Gate Park is open 5 a.m. to midnight.

name: SoMa West Skatepark
why: Opened in 2014 under the Central Freeway as part of a project that also added a dog park, its multi-level street course of hubbas, ledges, rails and stairs was designed to echo San Francisco street spots.
heads_up: Sits under the freeway deck and is lit, so evening sessions work.

name: Stoner Skate Plaza
why: Built by California Skateparks in Stoner Park in 2010, the West LA plaza recreates street spots that are gone or off-limits, with curved banks and ledges, stairs, a hubba and euro gaps, and it shows up in plenty of skate videos.
heads_up: Posted hours are short (listed as 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.), so check before a late session.

name: Sunset Dunes Skatepark
why: Opened June 27, 2025 at the south end of Sunset Dunes park by Sloat Boulevard, it was designed by Rec and Park with local skaters and fabricated by pro Austin Kanfoush's company, next to a pump track.
heads_up: Beginner-friendly and right on the ocean, so dress for wind.

name: The Cove Skatepark
why: Santa Monica's 20,000 sq ft park has a tile-coped pool, an over-vert bowl and the Douglas Park rail, in the town where the Dogtown crew first turned surf moves into skateboarding.
heads_up: Pay-to-skate with registration: buy a day, quarterly or annual pass before your first session.

name: Town Park (DeFremery Park)
why: Teacher and artist Keith "K-Dub" Williams began turning a vacant lot in West Oakland's DeFremery Park into Town Park in 2007; Levi's, California Skateparks and the city added a concrete section in 2014.
heads_up: A community park with a mix of concrete and wooden ramps, so it's friendly to beginners.

name: Truckee Bike Park
why: Three flow lines (beginner, intermediate and advanced) that you drop into and pump over berms and jumps, plus a side-by-side Dual Pump track and a start-to-finish Straight Rhythm line.
heads_up: Truckee is snow country, so expect a winter off-season; check conditions before you drive up.

name: UN Skate Plaza
why: When Civic Center's UN Plaza reopened in November 2023, roughly half of it became a street skate area, and skaters generally rate the design a success.
heads_up: A busy public plaza shared with markets and pedestrians, so skate with care.

name: Venice Beach Roller Skate Dance Plaza
why: The city opened this boardwalk plaza in 2000 for the roller skate dance scene that took off in Venice in the late 1970s; the Venice Beach Skate Dance Association keeps the weekend sessions and sound system going.
heads_up: A flat dance-skating spot, not a ramp park: sessions happen on weekends, so bring quads or inlines and join the circle.

name: Venice Beach Skatepark
why: Opened in October 2009 beside the Venice boardwalk, the 16,000 sq ft beachfront park is officially the Dennis "Polar Bear" Agnew Memorial Skatepark, named for a Z-Boys skater, with steps, rails and bowls shaped like empty swimming pools.
heads_up: Weekend afternoons are packed with skaters and boardwalk spectators; early mornings are calmer.

name: Verdugo Skate Park
why: Opened in April 2004, the 15,000 sq ft park packs a clover bowl with an over-vert section, a kidney pool, a street plaza and a snake run that drops into a bowl with a loveseat.
heads_up: Free for under-18s and Glendale residents; non-resident adults pay a small day fee (passes available).

name: Volcom Brothers Skatepark
why: Grindline built this 40,000 sq ft mountain park in 2006 around two big open bowls, one with an over-vert capsule, and a deep pocket bowl, with banks, ledges and rails around them.
heads_up: Seasonal: closed roughly November to May for snow; sunrise to sunset in summer, no lights.

name: Washington Street Skatepark
why: Skaters started building it under the highway at Washington Street in 1999, when San Diego had no public parks; the maze of bowls, spines and hips with an over-vert capsule has won Thrasher's T-Eddy for best park.
heads_up: The gate is padlocked and opens when a keyholder shows up, so times vary; expect kinks and steep lines.

name: West LA Courthouse Skate Plaza
why: Famous since the 1990s for the ledges around its tree boxes and a tall stage ledge, the courthouse plaza became a legal skate spot in 2014 after local skaters worked with the city and Nike SB.
heads_up: The civic site is slated for redevelopment and it reopened in February 2026 with temporary obstacles, so expect changes.

name: Arvada Skate Park
why: At 40,000 sq ft this Team Pain park was the largest on 5280's list of metro Denver parks, with roll-ins, a snake-like bowl system, a skateable brick wall, a half-bowl, stairs, ledges and a large ramp on an island.
heads_up: Lights stay on until 10 p.m.; mix of street and bowl lines means plenty of people crossing paths, so call your line.

name: Baldridge Park Skatepark
why: Built by Alltec in 1997, this 17,000 sq ft park drew skate magazine coverage for its concrete doughnut and volcano, and later added a 10-foot-deep bowl and a street course.
heads_up: The bowls are the draw: Westword called the later street course questionable.

name: Breckenridge Skate Park
why: Next to the Breckenridge Recreation Center at 880 Airport Road, the town park has an 11-foot bowl, a snake run, beginner and advanced bowls and a skateable historic mine cart, plus a 12,500 sq ft beginner expansion opened in September 2025.
heads_up: Open sunrise to sunset and only seasonally as conditions allow; there are no lights and snow shuts it in winter.

name: Carbondale Skatepark
why: Grindline built this 13,000 sq ft park in 2004 with pockets, pump bumps, tight vertical transitions and a large concrete capsule nicknamed God's Nostril; Westword once ranked it second in Colorado.
heads_up: Tight, fast transitions that punish mistakes; watch a few runs before you drop in.

name: Curbside Skatepark
why: Metro Denver's indoor option since 2018: an 11,000 sq ft warehouse park in Sheridan with a mini ramp, street features, a skate shop and board rentals, plus lessons, clinics and camps.
heads_up: Paid sessions (from $10 for two hours in 2022) and closed Mondays; hours vary, so check before you drive over.

name: Denver Skatepark
why: Opened in 2001 beside the South Platte River behind Union Station, this free park was billed as the largest public skatepark in the U.S. when it opened and grew to about 60,000 sq ft of bowls and street course; it hosted an X Games event and a Tony Hawk visit in its first year.
heads_up: Open 5 a.m. to 11 p.m. under lights; it gets packed on summer evenings and weekend afternoons, and the concrete runs slick, so weekday mornings are calmer.

name: Discovery Park Skatepark
why: A 13,000 sq ft Team Pain park at West 38th and Kipling with a three-section bowl with gaps and roll-ins, a flow section of street features, a manual box and a pyramid; 5280 rates it beginner-friendly, with Front Range views.
heads_up: A good place to learn bowl basics; it is small, so take turns when it is busy.

name: Don Anema Memorial Skate Park
why: A Team Pain flow park opened in 2011 and built for nonstop lines: arches beside gaps, a spiral roll-in bowl, snake-like ramps, manual boxes, stairs, ledges and a large back bowl.
heads_up: Flow parks mean long lines crossing each other; watch the traffic before you drop in.

name: Fossil Creek Skate Park
why: This 12,000 sq ft plaza, built by Alltec Skateparks in 2004, mimics real street spots with gaps, rails, manual pads and stairs of varying heights and no transitions.
heads_up: No transition at all; bring a street setup.

name: Railbender Skate Park
why: Opened in 2008 and designed by Site Design Group, this 35,000 sq ft park leans toward street skating with ledges, stairs and manual boxes, but also has steep roll-ins, a smooth mini bowl and a large, complex bowl.
heads_up: Lights come on at dusk and go off at 10 p.m.

name: Rio Grande Skatepark
why: Team Pain built this downtown Aspen park with the city in 2000: 17,000 sq ft of big and small bowls, a spine ramp and a 10-foot vert wall with pool coping, and Westword once ranked it third in its Colorado top ten.
heads_up: Mountain-town park: snow closes it in winter, so plan on the late-spring-to-fall season.

name: Trinidad Skatepark (Southside Park)
why: Grindline finished this 14,000 sq ft park in early 2003, twice its planned size thanks to donated concrete and rebar, with a shallow winding start, hips and corners and a deep rectangular bowl; Westword once ranked it first in Colorado.
heads_up: Out-of-the-way southern Colorado town, so bring water and plan food stops on the drive.

name: Ulysses Skatepark
why: Team Pain built this 27,000 sq ft park with a big, slightly downhill carving bowl, stairs, ledges, quarter pipes, a manual box and a tunnel with Golden's name carved in its roof, all with foothills views.
heads_up: Lights go off at 10 p.m.; it is reached by a path of almost half a mile along the neighbouring dog park.

name: West Lake Skatepark
why: This 18,000 sq ft city park has three sizable concrete bowls plus a street area with rails, walls and ramps; the city is also planning a destination wheel park at Emerson Park with Team Pain.
heads_up: Western Slope desert sun: bring water in summer and skate early or late.

name: Wheel Park Skatepark
why: SITE Design Group built this 20,000 sq ft park in 2002 with a mellow street course of ledges and rails, a snake run and two fast bowls.
heads_up: Skaters only (no bikes); the bowls sit close together and get crowded on weekends, so go on weekday mornings or before noon.

name: Zeke M. Pierce Skatepark
why: A free street park of rails and stairs tucked into one of Vail's town parking structures, easy to miss but handy between mountain sessions.
heads_up: Lit and open until 11 p.m. in season, but it is snowed out in winter (OpenStreetMap lists it closed December to February).

name: Rockwell Skatepark
why: An 18,000 sq ft concrete park in Rockwell Park designed by Site Design Group and built by California Skateparks, with a bowl that runs from a shallow to a deep end, stairs, hubbas and a bench-over-gap.
heads_up: Unsupervised city park — the deep end of the bowl is for confident riders.

name: Scalzi Skatepark
why: A 10,000 sq ft Grindline park built in 2007 in Scalzi Park, with transitions, hips, transfers, an over-vert section and pool coping alongside a small street area.
heads_up: Tight, transition-heavy layout — the over-vert section is for experienced riders.

name: Bethune Point Skatepark
why: A 16,000-square-foot Spohn Ranch park on the Halifax River (2009) whose kidney bowl is built as a replica of a 1970s California backyard pool, with blue tile and pool coping, next to a street section around a 'broken pyramid'.
heads_up: Skaters under 18 need a waiver signed by a parent or guardian before they can ride.

name: Blake Doyle Skatepark
why: About 25,000 square feet of concrete under Interstate 110 in the Hollice T. Williams greenway, opened in May 2023 and built by Evergreen Skateparks, with a beginner area, a multilevel plaza and two bowls.
heads_up: Start in the beginner section if you are new to concrete.

name: Bro Bowl (Perry Harvey Sr. Park)
why: Opened in 1979 as Florida's first public skatepark, the Bro Bowl became the first skatepark listed on the U.S. National Register of Historic Places (2013); the original was demolished in the park's renovation and replaced by a new bowl closely modelled on it.
heads_up: Banked 1970s-style shapes reward carving more than tech tricks; go early or late to avoid the midday heat.

name: Kona Skatepark
why: Opened in June 1977 in Arlington, Kona is listed by Guinness World Records as the oldest surviving commercial skatepark; its original snake and J-runs are still ridden alongside a pro bowl, vert ramp, mini ramp and street course.
heads_up: Private paid park, open noon to 9 p.m. and closed Mondays; the vert ramp needed a rebuild in 2024, so ask what is open.

name: Lot 11 Skatepark
why: A 38,000-square-foot concrete park under the I-95 bridge near downtown Miami, opened in 2019 and built by American Ramp Company and Pivot Custom, with a combi bowl (pool coping and tile) wrapped by a large street plaza with granite ledges.
heads_up: Busy in the evenings when it cools down; posted hours have changed over time, so check before a late session.

name: Pompano Beach Skatepark
why: The City of Pompano Beach's concrete park in Community Park, designed and built by New Line Skateparks and opened on July 22, 2026, with street and transition terrain and a skateable Pompano fish sculpture.
heads_up: Posted rules require a strapped helmet, closed-toe shoes and a shirt; open 8 a.m. to 10 p.m.

name: Possum Creek Skatepark
why: An 18,000-square-foot Spohn Ranch park (2009) laid out as a triangle, with a waterfall bowl in one corner and several stair sets with hubbas and handrails through the middle.
heads_up: No lights: open sunrise to sunset only.

name: Skatepark of Tampa (SPoT)
why: Open to the public since January 1993, SPoT hosts the Tampa Pro (first held in 1995) and the Tampa Am, and its street course is rebuilt every year for the contests; there is also an outdoor concrete transition course and a beginner course.
heads_up: Paid sessions with a signed waiver; check the posted hours before you go, especially around contest weeks.

name: Bay Creek Skatepark
why: A 12,000-square-foot park designed and built by Pillar Design Studios in 2009 with local skaters, where a central platform links a bowl, mini ramp and volcano to a street plaza of stairs, hubbas and handrails.
heads_up: Open sunrise to 11 p.m. with lights.

name: Brook Run Skate Park
why: A 27,000-square-foot lighted park opened in 2007, run by the City of Dunwoody since 2010 and free since 2011, with a flow bowl, a tiled pool-style bowl and a street section.
heads_up: The gate opens at 7 a.m.; lights allow evening sessions.

name: Central City Skatepark
why: A free public park in downtown Macon with a street section that opened in 2017 and a concrete bowl added in 2019.
heads_up: Summer afternoons are hot; go early or late.

name: Duncan Creek Park Skatepark
why: A 20,000-square-foot Wally Hollyday park (2008) in Gwinnett County with six bowls, including a backyard-style pool, plus four stair sets with rails and ledges.
heads_up: The deep pool is for confident transition skaters; warm up in the smaller bowls first.

name: Historic Fourth Ward Skatepark
why: Atlanta's first free public skatepark (2011), a 17,000-square-foot Pillar Design Studios park beside the BeltLine with a rocket-shaped bowl, two more open bowls and a street plaza, helped by a $25,000 Tony Hawk Foundation grant.
heads_up: Open sunrise to 11 p.m. with lights.

name: Kona Skatepark
why: Built in phases by the community at Old Kona Airport park on Kuakini Highway from a Dreamland Skateparks master plan, it has a street course around a big pyramid, stairs and ledges, plus flow bowls and quarterpipes.
heads_up: Not the historic 1977 Kona Skatepark, which is in Jacksonville, Florida; skate early or late to dodge the midday sun.

name: Fort Boise Skatepark
why: Opened in 1999 and designed by local skaters with the City of Boise, with help from Prestige Skateshop, it was the first park in Boise built specifically for skateboarding.
heads_up: Boise winters bring snow and ice; it is a dry-season park.

name: Rhodes Skate Park
why: Built under the I-184 connector by former highway commissioner Glenn Rhodes with more than 130 volunteers and dedicated in 1995, it was rebuilt by Grindline with a $1.25 million Albertson Family Foundation gift and reopened in April 2016.
heads_up: Open sunrise to 11 p.m.; no e-scooters or motorized vehicles. Grindline says it gets more use per square foot than any other Boise park, so expect company.

name: Grant Skate Park
why: The Chicago Park District's free skate park in the south end of Grant Park at 1135 S. Michigan Avenue, a concrete park a short ride from the Loop.
heads_up: Downtown lakefront park; wind off the lake can be strong.

name: Iles Park Skatepark
why: A 5,000-square-foot Spohn Ranch plaza (2021) for the Springfield Park District, with ledges, stairs, a manual pad, handrails and a flat bar designed with local skaters.
heads_up: Helmets and pads are strongly encouraged at Springfield Park District skateparks.

name: Logan Boulevard Skate Park
why: A 1.29-acre Chicago Park District park beneath the Kennedy Expressway in Logan Square, with a bowl corner with a spine, quarters with hips, a funbox with rails and a manual pad, shared by skaters and BMX riders.
heads_up: Covered by the expressway, so it often stays skateable in the rain; local groups have proposed a renovation, so check for construction.

name: Wilson Skate Park
why: A free Chicago Park District skate park at 700 W. Wilson Avenue on the lakefront near Montrose Beach.
heads_up: Lakefront spot near Montrose Beach, so wind can be strong.

name: Griffin Bike Park
why: A 300-acre bike park with more than two dozen lines. They run from the one-mile, all-ability Basic Training Skills Loop of berms and hips to Mega Pump, an expert 0.6-mile pump trail with three big jumps.
heads_up: OpenStreetMap lists it as open 24/7 "weather permitting", so check conditions after rain.

name: Major Taylor Skate Park
why: Indy Parks' skate park at the Lake Sullivan Sports Complex, built in 1999 next to the Major Taylor Velodrome and BMX track, open to skateboarders, inline skaters and cyclists.
heads_up: Shared with bikes and inline skaters; the velodrome and BMX track next door are run separately.

name: Sunset Skatepark
why: Opened in December 2023 on the Ohio River levee, this 27,000-square-foot Hunger Skateparks all-wheels park has a hybrid roller rink and skate zone, a flow bowl, a pool bowl, long adaptive ledges and street areas.
heads_up: Built for all wheels, so expect roller skaters and BMX alongside skateboards.

name: Willard Park Skatepark
why: Designed by Hunger Skateparks and pushed through by Indy Skatepark Advocates, this park near downtown is the largest the city has built and its first new outdoor park since 1999, with a flow bowl and a street plaza.
heads_up: No lights: dawn to dusk.

name: Lauridsen Skatepark
why: Opened in May 2021 on the Des Moines riverfront, this 88,000-square-foot park was the largest public skatepark in the U.S. when it opened and hosted Dew Tour 2021, with park and street courses, a flow bowl, an amoeba pool and a snake run.
heads_up: Open 6 a.m. to 10:30 p.m. with lights; helmets and pads are highly recommended, and BMX riders must use plastic pegs.

name: Riverside Skatepark
why: An 8,500-square-foot Spohn Ranch concrete park opened in 2020 to replace a flood-destroyed wooden park, built behind the levee, with a mini ramp, a five-stair with rail and hubba, and street features.
heads_up: No lights: sunrise to sunset.

name: Young's Park Skatepark
why: An 8,000-square-foot Spohn Ranch park (2018) that replaced an old set of wood and metal ramps, with a split bowl (4-foot and 6-foot sections) and a compact street area.
heads_up: Open dawn to dusk.

name: Berry Hill Park Skatepark
why: An 18,000-square-foot Lexington city park with a flow bowl and snake run, horseshoe-stamped concrete and metal rails with thoroughbred designs.
heads_up: Open dawn to dusk.

name: David Armstrong Extreme Park
why: Opened in 2002 near downtown Louisville, this 40,000-square-foot park has a 24-foot full pipe, bowls from 4 to 11 feet, a 12-foot wooden vert ramp and a street course; part of it was rebuilt in 2015 after bridge construction.
heads_up: Closes at 11 p.m. nightly (cameras enforce it); the full pipe and 11-foot bowls are for experienced riders.

name: Newport DIY Skatepark
why: Volunteer-built DIY terrain under the I-471 bridge, across the river from Cincinnati, that local skaters and Galaxie Skateshop have grown since about 2008, with a concrete bowl poured by Hunger Skateparks in 2017.
heads_up: Not a city park: it is kept up by volunteers, so respect the locals, take your trash and consider chipping in to the build fund.

name: Woodland Skatepark
why: A roughly 12,000-square-foot park in Woodland Park on East High Street near downtown Lexington, with bowls, ramps and pyramids.
heads_up: Skateboards only: no bikes or scooters; open dawn to dusk.

name: Houma Skatepark (Fireman's Skate and Bike Park)
why: A 15,000-square-foot Spohn Ranch park opened in 2015, started with a $10,000 bequest from a local man named Jerry, with an open bowl and a full street section.
heads_up: No lights: sunrise to sunset.

name: Parisite Skatepark
why: Started by the Parisite DIY crew building ramps and concrete without permission under the I-610 overpass on Pleasure Street, then legitimised with the city and state and rebuilt with Spohn Ranch as a 6,000-square-foot concrete park in 2014.
heads_up: No lights (sunrise to sunset); respect the local crew who fought for the spot.

name: Dougherty Field Skatepark
why: Portland's city skatepark at Dougherty Field, recently expanded with new concrete areas designed with Pillar Design and built with Artisan Skateparks.
heads_up: Fresh concrete and grass were still settling after the expansion — stay off fenced or seeded areas.

name: Greenbelt Skatepark
