why: A 7,000 sq ft California Skateparks build with a 10.5-ft peanut bowl with pool coping, a kidney bowl, banks, hips and ledges.
heads_up: Bowl-first park — the peanut bowl's deep end is 10.5 ft.

name: Hagerstown Skatepark
why: A Spohn Ranch park opened in 2022 with a mini ramp, a flow bowl, ledges and a skateable 'H' sculpture, plus a pump track.
heads_up: Open sunrise to sunset.

name: Ocean Bowl Skatepark
why: Opened in June 1976 as the first skatepark on the East Coast and described as the longest-running municipal skatepark in the US; it was rebuilt on the same site in 1998 and has hosted the Dew Tour.
heads_up: Resort-town park — check the town's hours and admission before you go.

name: Olney Manor Skatepark
why: A 14,400 sq ft Montgomery County park designed by Site Design Group and built by California Skateparks, with a 10-ft bowl with pool coping and a street section.
heads_up: Open daytime hours; the 10-ft bowl is the deep end — mind it.

name: Skatepark of Baltimore
why: An 11,000 sq ft concrete park in Roosevelt Park in Hampden, opened in 2016, with deep bowls, stairs, ledges and a small handrail.
heads_up: Daytime hours only; the deep bowls are not for first-timers.

name: Lynch Family Skatepark
why: About 40,000 sq ft beneath the Zakim Bridge ramps, opened in 2015 after a long Charles River Conservancy campaign; Stantec designed it and California Skateparks built it, with three bowls up to about 11.5 ft deep and a street plaza.
heads_up: Partly covered by the highway, so some lines stay dry in light rain; BMX, inline and scooters are allowed too, so share the bowls.

name: North Adams Skatepark (Unity Skate Park)
why: An 11,000 sq ft Spohn Ranch street park built in 2017 in the Berkshires, with down, out and flat ledges, handrails, stairs, a pole jam and a euro gap.
heads_up: Mostly street terrain — bring your ledge game rather than your bowl board.

name: Oak Crest Cove Skatepark
why: Cape Cod concrete park opened in 2020 with a flow bowl, a 6–9 ft amoeba bowl with extensions and hips, and a street area with ledges, manual pads and rails.
heads_up: The amoeba bowl reaches 9 ft at its deepest — know your transition.

name: Ann Arbor Skatepark
why: A 30,000-square-foot park in Veterans Memorial Park that opened in June 2014 after years of local advocacy, with a kidney bowl, a clover bowl, a snake run and a street course; Tony Hawk skated the opening.
heads_up: Friends of the Ann Arbor Skatepark run free All Girls Skate sessions on some Sunday mornings in season.

name: Ferndale Skatepark (Donald Red Geary Skatepark)
why: An 18,000-square-foot Evergreen Skateparks park opened in 2019 with help from a $250,000 Tony Hawk Foundation grant, with an open bowl, a spine, hubbas and flat rails.
heads_up: Open 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. as weather permits.

name: Marquette Skate Plaza
why: A 9,000-square-foot Upper Peninsula plaza at Pine Street and Fair Avenue, built by Spohn Ranch after a seven-year community fundraising campaign, with a California-style high bank and a Barcelona-style wall.
heads_up: Upper Peninsula winters are long; the season runs roughly late spring to fall.

name: Modern Skate Park
why: Modern Skate & Surf's indoor park, which the shop lists at 60,000 square feet, opened in 2008 with more than an acre of ramps and rails, including a wooden bowl built by Team Pain.
heads_up: Runs set session times with an electronic waiver; check the schedule before you drive over.

name: Ranney Skate Park
why: A 20,000-square-foot Team Pain park in Ranney Park with quarter pipes and a vert extension, a 5-to-9-foot egg bowl, a large pyramid and transfer gaps.
heads_up: Lit for evening sessions; the egg bowl's deep end is for confident skaters.

name: Ride It Sculpture Park
why: A free skatepark and art project on four vacant lots along the Davison Freeway at Klinger Street, started in 2012 by Power House Productions with visiting skaters and artists and expanded by Evergreen Skateparks in 2013 and 2017.
heads_up: Neighbourhood art space, not a city park: be respectful of the residents on the block.

name: Riverside Park Skatepark
why: A 21,000-square-foot Grindline park on the Detroit riverfront (2019) with two stair sets with handrails, a hubba, a pole jam, banks and a central pool-style bowl.
heads_up: Riverfront wind makes it cold in spring and fall; dress for it.

name: Sterling Heights Skatepark
why: A 20,000-square-foot Evergreen Skateparks park opened in 2018 with the city and local skaters, mixing a bowl and quarter pipes with stairs, rails and a manual pad.
heads_up: No lights; open 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. April to September, with shorter hours the rest of the year.

name: 3rd Lair Skatepark
why: Founded in the late 1990s by Mark Muller, 3rd Lair is a skate shop and indoor park that is one of the most popular in Minnesota, with a peanut bowl, a vert ramp, a mini-ramp room and street terrain, plus an outdoor area.
heads_up: The main winter option in the Twin Cities; check session times and waiver rules before you go.

name: Bemidji Skate Plaza
why: A 14,000-square-foot concrete plaza in City Park built by Spohn Ranch to a SITE Design Group plan and opened in November 2010, which Spohn describes as Minnesota's first public skate plaza; it has a China Banks replica, a snake run and a bowl.
heads_up: Northern Minnesota season is short: expect snow cover from late fall into spring.

name: JXTA Skate-Able Art Plaza
why: A 4,200-square-foot plaza on West Broadway designed by Juxtaposition Arts' youth apprentices and built by Hunger Skateparks in 2019, which the Cultural Landscape Foundation calls the first public skatepark in Minneapolis.
heads_up: Small and unlit; it is an art plaza, so be mindful of people using the space.

name: Keene Creek Bike Park
why: Built by volunteers with COGGS (Cyclists of Gitchee Gumee Shores) on about an acre near and partly under Interstate 35. It has a dirt jump plaza with beginner, intermediate and advanced lines, a pump track, and a bike playground of wooden features.
heads_up: Parts of the park are still being built; the city lists the beginner, intermediate and advanced jump lines as open.

name: Pidgeon Park (Hernando Skatepark)
why: A 6,000-square-foot Evergreen Skateparks concrete park in Renasant Park (2015), about 30 minutes south of Memphis, named for Edward Pidgeon, who raised the money for it at the farmers market for years.
heads_up: No lights; plan for daylight sessions.

name: Kinetic Park
why: This St. Charles County park, formerly the Youth Activity Park, has what the county billed as the largest asphalt pump track in the nation. It hosted Red Bull UCI Pump Track World Championships qualifiers in 2021 and 2022.
heads_up: OpenStreetMap lists the park as open 10 a.m. to 10 p.m. daily; check St. Charles County Parks for current hours.

name: MOmentum Bike Park
why: A new city bike park in its first season in 2026. Joplin is one of four US communities hosting a 2026 Velosolutions/UCI Pump Track qualifier, held at the park on August 15–16, 2026.
heads_up: OpenStreetMap lists it as open 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.; the park is brand new, so check with the City of Joplin for current details.

name: Penn Valley Skate Park
why: Opened in 2005 on the hill in Penn Valley Park overlooking downtown Kansas City, it pairs a bank-heavy street plaza with a bowl that waterfalls from 6 to 9 feet with real pool coping and tile.
heads_up: Steady local crowd; the bowl's deep end is for confident transition skaters.

name: Westhoff Plaza Skate and BMX Complex
why: A concrete skate and BMX park in Westhoff Park in St. Louis's western suburbs, opened by the city in 2012, with ledges, a stair set, hubbas, a jump gap and a six-foot bowl.
heads_up: Closes for rain, ice and snow; in winter the closing time depends on the temperature.

name: Anthem Skatepark
why: Henderson's Anthem park pairs a kidney pool that runs from 5 to 8 feet deep and an 8-foot square bowl with a flow course of pockets and a street course of ledges, rails and a fun box.
heads_up: South end of the valley; desert heat applies, so go early or late.

name: Craig Ranch Skatepark
why: Opened in October 2013 inside Craig Ranch Regional Park, this free concrete park of more than 60,000 sq ft was the largest in the Las Vegas Valley when it opened, with big, medium and small bowls plus ledges, stairs, rails and hubbas.
heads_up: Open 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. with lights for night sessions; bring water, as summer days are extreme.

name: Desert Breeze Skatepark
why: Clark County's concrete park at Desert Breeze Park on Spring Mountain Road hosted a stop of the Tony Hawk tour (Extreme Thing) and is built mainly for intermediate and advanced skaters, with some beginner areas.
heads_up: Lights run on a timer; summer days are brutally hot, so skate early or after dark.

name: Hollywood Skatepark
why: Clark County's advanced park: about 29,000 sq ft designed by SITE Design Group with an 11-foot kidney bowl, an 18-foot full pipe and a street plaza with a 10-stair.
heads_up: Supervised park, open only during set hours (2:30-9 p.m. weekdays, 9 a.m.-9 p.m. weekends) with a small entry fee; check the county schedule.

name: Jaycee Skatepark
why: A 10,000 sq ft SITE Design Group street park in central Las Vegas with long stair sets, handrails, hubbas, bank-to-ledge, a taco quarter pipe with pool coping and a floating corner bowl.
heads_up: Listed as open 24 hours and well lit, which makes it the night-session spot in summer.

name: Police Memorial Skatepark
why: A northwest Las Vegas park that mixes a street section of stair sets, rails, hubbas, ledges, bank ramps and a pyramid with transition of quarter pipes and a spine.
heads_up: Open 7 a.m. to 11 p.m. with lights, so summer sessions can wait for sundown.

name: Chris Rice Skateboard Park
why: Portsmouth's skatepark on Greenland Road, opened December 21, 2023, next to the Seacoast Greenway and the city bike park; volunteers added a pump track beside it in 2024.
heads_up: Lit in the evening: the lights dim 30 and 15 minutes before closing and switch off at close; no e-bikes, e-scooters or electric boards on the surface.

name: David W. Deane Skateboard Park
why: A 20,000 sq ft Pillar Design and Artisan Skateparks build with two pool-style bowls, extensions, hips, volcanoes and a keyhole, plus ledges and a kicker with a fire hydrant.
heads_up: Transition-heavy park — the pool-style bowls are the main event.

name: Red Alert Skatepark
why: Indoor park and skate shop in downtown Rochester with quarter pipes, banks, rails, ledges, a pyramid, a euro gap and a mini ramp — one of the few places to skate indoors in New Hampshire.
heads_up: Paid sessions — check the shop's current hours and rates before driving in.

name: Berry Lane Skatepark
why: A 12,000 sq ft park that reopened in 2020 as part of the Berry Lane Park rebuild, pairing a street course (flat bars, stair sets, a camel hump) with a flow bowl.
heads_up: Part of a larger rebuilt city park; check Jersey City recreation for current hours.

name: Ocean City Skatepark
why: A 12,000 sq ft Spohn Ranch park in the Jersey Shore resort town, with a flow bowl, a snake run, hubba ledges, a four-stair and a mini ramp.
heads_up: Shore town in summer — check the city for hours and any pass or fee before you go.

name: Seven Presidents Skatepark
why: Oceanfront Spohn Ranch park of about 21,000 sq ft in Seven Presidents Oceanfront Park, rebuilt after Hurricane Sandy and later expanded with a second flow bowl.
heads_up: Beachfront park — summer beach traffic and parking can be tight; check hours and any fee before you go.

name: Toms River Skatepark
why: A 7,000 sq ft Spohn Ranch park built in 2021, with a bowl that runs from a 4-ft shallow end to a 6-ft deep end, a half pyramid, a hubba ledge and a euro gap.
heads_up: Listed as open 24/7, but it's unstaffed — skate with a friend after dark.

name: Alix Rice Peace Park Skatepark
why: Grindline-built park just outside Buffalo with a flow bowl (waterfall, extension and radial pocket), a separate pool and a street section with stairs, a hubba, a handrail and a round manual pad.
heads_up: Outdoor concrete — the pool and flow bowl need time to dry out after rain.

name: Andy Kessler Skatepark
why: Manhattan's first full-size public skatepark, built in 1995–96 by Andy Kessler with local teens in Riverside Park; rebuilt in concrete by California Skateparks in 2019 with a street plaza, a 4-ft mini ramp and an 11-ft pool with pool coping.
heads_up: In Riverside Park at 108th Street; the pool's deep end has 18 inches of vert.

name: Brooklyn Banks
why: The wave-like brick banks under the Manhattan side of the Brooklyn Bridge were a cornerstone of New York street skating until they closed for bridge work in 2010; the big banks reopened to the public on June 5, 2025, with skate space developed alongside Gotham Park and The Skatepark Project.
heads_up: The city has budgeted a further rebuild of the space under the bridge (The Arches), so check for construction fencing before you make the trip.

name: Golconda Skate Park (Fat Kid Spot)
why: Started as the DIY 'Fat Kid Spot' under the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway near DUMBO and reopened in 2016 as an 18,000 sq ft concrete and brick park designed with advice from Steve Rodriguez.
heads_up: Locals and the NYC Skateboard Coalition keep a tool box on site and hold monthly clean-ups, so grab a broom if the surface is dusty; the expressway overhead gives some cover.

name: Lower East Side Skatepark (Coleman Playground)
why: Concrete park under the Manhattan Bridge, rebuilt in 2012 to a design donated by Steve Rodriguez and built by California Skateparks; its central location makes it a regular stop for jams, demos and best-trick contests.
heads_up: NYC Parks requires a helmet plus knee and elbow pads here; open dawn to dusk, and the bridge overhead keeps parts of it dry in light rain.

name: Millennium Skate Park (Owl's Head)
why: Brooklyn's first concrete skatepark, opened in 2001 in Owl's Head Park in Bay Ridge and designed by Andy Kessler; about 14,000 sq ft with a street section and bowls up to 8 ft deep.
heads_up: Helmet rule is enforced; the NYC Skateboard Coalition holds a yearly pool-series event here, which fills the bowl.

name: Montauk Skate Park
why: A 20,000 sq ft concrete park opened in 2022 by American Ramp Company and Pivot Customs, with a flow bowl, a snake run, a bowl with pool coping and a full street section at the tip of Long Island.
heads_up: Outdoor concrete at the far end of Long Island — check the forecast before making the drive.

name: Mullaly Skate Park
why: Installed in 1988 in Mullaly Park on 164th Street near Yankee Stadium, it is one of New York City's first public skateparks.
heads_up: Sits between Jerome and River Avenues by Yankee Stadium; check NYC Parks for current hours and rules.

name: Pier 62 Skatepark
why: Opened in May 2010 on a Hudson River Park pier in Chelsea, this 15,000 sq ft concrete park by California Skateparks and Site Design Group has a 10-foot pool that runs to vert, a flow area with a clamshell and a small street section.
heads_up: Open 8 a.m. to dusk; the deep end of the pool is 10 ft, so know your transition before you drop in.

name: ROC City Skatepark
why: Built under the Frederick Douglass–Susan B. Anthony Bridge after a nearly 20-year effort by local skaters and the city; Phase 1, focused on transition, opened in fall 2020, and a 13,000 sq ft street plaza (Phase 2) was set to follow.
heads_up: Phase 2 construction next door was scheduled to finish in fall 2026 — expect fencing on the south side until it opens.

name: Rockaway Beach Skatepark
why: Beachside park by the Rockaway boardwalk at Beach 91st Street; the worn wooden original, battered by a hurricane, was replaced with a concrete park with a triple-set hubba, ledges and a transition section off to the side.
heads_up: Little standing room except the edges, and scooter riders favour the kicker-ledge bank — expect to share lines.

name: Tompkins Square Park
why: A paved corner of this East Village park has been a daily flatground and meeting spot for New York skaters for decades; in 2019 NYC Parks dropped a plan to turf it after a petition gathered more than 32,000 signatures.
heads_up: It's a shared public park, not a built skatepark — mostly flat ground, so give other park users room.

name: Atlantic Beach Skatepark
why: A 13,000-square-foot park in Atlantic Beach Town Park by Pillar Design Studios and Artisan Skateparks, with a bowl with pool coping and a street section a short walk from the beach.
heads_up: Seasonal hours: weekends only before and after summer, daily 10 a.m.-10 p.m. in summer; check the town's parks page.

name: Cherokee Action Sports Park
why: Funded by the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians and opened in June 2011 on Acquoni Road, this Pillar-designed, Artisan-built park of about 13,000 square feet has a vert bowl with pool coping, a flow bowl and street features.
heads_up: Older concrete shows some wear; mountain weather changes quickly, so expect wet patches after storms.

name: Durham Skate Park
why: A 10,000-square-foot downtown park on Foster Street by Pillar Design Studios and Artisan Skateparks, mixing a backyard-style bowl with a street plaza.
heads_up: Listed as open dawn to dusk.

name: George Poston Park Pump Track
why: North Carolina's first Velosolutions pump track, about 10,000 sq ft, in a Gaston County park that also has more than 10 miles of singletrack. It hosted Red Bull UCI Pump Track World Championships qualifiers, including in 2021 and 2022.
heads_up: The coordinates mark the park as a whole; the pump track is one part of a larger park with trails.

name: Marsh Creek Skatepark
why: A 12,000-square-foot Pillar Design Studios park (2009) inside the 110-acre Marsh Creek Park, with a large bowl, a snake run and street obstacles.
heads_up: No lights: sunrise to sunset only.

name: Mooresville Skatepark
why: Opened in December 2022 north of Charlotte, this park designed by Team Pain and built by Artisan Skateparks for just under $3 million has an amoeba bowl and a square bowl with pool coping, a shallow snake run and a street section.
heads_up: Check Mooresville Parks and Recreation for current hours.

name: Athens Skate Park
why: Built by Grindline in 2003 behind the Athens Recreation Center, this park was once the only one with a 'capsule' (a full 16-foot pipe connected to a cradle) and is among the largest concrete parks in Ohio.
heads_up: Older Grindline concrete with cement coping; the capsule is for experienced riders.

name: Camp Washington Skatepark
why: Cincinnati's first public skatepark, about 15,500 square feet by Hunger Skateparks beside the Camp Washington Recreation Area, opened in August 2026 with a bowl from 3.5 to 8 feet, a tech alley, a flow street pit and street features.
heads_up: Open daily 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.; brand-new, so expect crowds in its first season.

name: Crooked River Skatepark
why: A Grindline park in Rivergate Park on the Cuyahoga River, built in 2014 with Tony Hawk Foundation support, with a flow bowl with hips and extensions, a pool-style bowl about 6 feet deep, stairs, rails and hubbas.
heads_up: Open 7 a.m. to 11 p.m. with lights for night sessions and restrooms on site.

name: Dayton Bike Yard
why: A newer bike park in Welcome Park with about 2.5 acres of jumps, a pump track, and areas set aside for beginners and families.
heads_up: The coordinates mark the pump track; the jump areas fill the rest of the 2.5-acre site.

name: Everett Park Skatepark
why: A Spohn Ranch concrete park of about 15,000 square feet with an elongated bowl that runs through a full pipe in the middle, plus a street plaza and a pump track.
heads_up: Open dawn to 11 p.m. with lights.

name: Mike's Bike Park
why: Two floors of indoor riding in a former downtown radiator factory, opened in 2016 by Mike Bisig. It has a pump track, jumps, ramps, skinnies, a foam pit, a cross-country loop and a beginner section, and almost anything without a motor is allowed.
heads_up: Open year-round; everyone signs a waiver before riding.

name: Ray's MTB Indoor Park
why: Opened in 2004 in a former factory on Cleveland's west side and since grown to about 165,000 sq ft. It has a full-size indoor pump track, a jump trail, foam pits, a BMX pool, and a trail of nearly a mile with rocks and logs built to feel like the woods.
heads_up: Seasonal: usually open October to April and closed in summer; riders under 18 need a waiver signed by a parent.

name: Rob Dyrdek/DC Shoes Skate Plaza
why: A gift from pro skater Rob Dyrdek, this large concrete plaza is built like a city square, with street terrain modelled on spots in Los Angeles, San Francisco and Barcelona.
heads_up: Open sunrise to sunset.

name: Ashland Skate Park
why: Opened in 1999 beside a creek at Water and Hersey streets, the roughly 15,000 sq ft park has a mini snake run, pyramids, a 6-foot bowl and a set of three connected bowls from 4 to 9 feet deep.
heads_up: Open sunrise to sunset; bikes are allowed.

name: Burnside Skatepark
why: Skaters began pouring concrete against a wall under the east end of the Burnside Bridge on Halloween night 1990, without permission; the city later accepted it, and the donation-funded DIY with hips, pools and vertical walls is regarded as the first DIY park.
heads_up: Steep, tight transitions and a strong local crew, so watch a few runs before you drop in.

name: Chehalem Skatepark
why: Dreamland built the 29,000 sq ft park in Ewing Young Park in 2000 after a petition from local middle schoolers; it hosted a stop of Tony Hawk's Gigantic Skatepark Tour in 2001 and has drop-ins from one foot to 13 feet around its volcano.
heads_up: Good for every level, from small rollers to 13-foot drops.

name: Commonwealth Skateboarding
why: An indoor park and skate shop on SE 20th Avenue that has kept Portland skating through the rain for more than 15 years, with several bowls, ramps, banks and a small street section in about 4,500 sq ft.
heads_up: Indoor and paid, so it's the rainy-day option; check session times before you go.

name: Ed Benedict Skate Plaza
why: Designed by Newline as one of the Northwest's first green skateparks, with stormwater filtration, the 18,000 sq ft street plaza in Ed Benedict Park has ledges, stairs, rails and banks.
heads_up: Street-only terrain, with no bowls.

name: Glenhaven Skatepark
why: An 11,000 sq ft Dreamland park in a Portland Parks sports complex, split between a 5,500 sq ft street course and a transition area with a nine-foot-deep peanut bowl.
heads_up: Outdoor and unroofed, so it's a dry-day spot in Portland's rainy season.

name: Lincoln City Skate Park
why: Dreamland Skateparks started it in 1999 and the coastal park now has four bowls: the Moguls Bowl, a covered cradle and half-pipe, a tight-transition swimming pool and the snake run.
heads_up: Skateboards only (no bikes, scooters or inlines); dawn to dusk; under-16s must wear helmets.

name: Pacific City Skatepark
why: A community-funded park near Cape Kiwanda designed by Dreamland Skateparks, with phase one breaking ground in February 2021; its design includes a brick bank, a wave-like ridge and an old dory boat set into the concrete.
heads_up: Built in phases as money comes in, so check what is open before a trip.

name: Pier Park Skatepark
why: Opened in 2006 in St. Johns, this Dreamland park packs four large bowls, an 18-foot full pipe with a mouse hole, flow bowls and a street section into about 11,500 sq ft.
heads_up: The full pipe and deep bowls are for confident skaters; the street section is the place to warm up.

name: Prineville Skatepark
why: Dreamland's 13,000 sq ft park in Ochoco Creek Park opened in summer 2019 with a flow area, pump bumps, quarterpipes, a handrail, a bowl and ledges, next to a dirt pump track.
heads_up: There's a playground right beside it, so watch for small kids.

name: Rockridge Skatepark
why: Built by Evergreen and run by Bend Parks & Recreation, the 11,000 sq ft park has a lunar-landscape layout of pump bumps, hips and bowls.
heads_up: Central Oregon winters can leave it snowed over; best from spring to fall.

name: WJ Skatepark + Urban Plaza
why: Dreamland built this 23,000 sq ft park under the I-105 bridge in 2014; the city calls it the country's largest covered and lighted public skatepark, with street and transition terrain.
heads_up: Open 6 a.m. to 1 a.m. and sheltered from rain by the bridge; under-16s must wear helmets.

name: Bethlehem SkatePlaza
why: A 23,000 sq ft street plaza on the South Bethlehem Greenway that stretches more than 750 ft and recreates city obstacles — handrails, benches, staircases and sculptures.
heads_up: Open dawn to dusk every day, weather permitting; it's across from the Wind Creek casino on Steel Avenue.

name: FDR Skatepark
why: Skater-built concrete under I-95 in South Philadelphia's FDR Park, grown since the mid-1990s with volunteer labour and donated materials; it hosted the 2005 Gravity Games and still runs on upkeep paid for by the people who skate it.
heads_up: Steep, homemade transitions — watch a few runs before you jump in; the highway overhead keeps much of it dry, and donations to the upkeep crew are welcome.

name: Paine's Park
why: About 30,000 sq ft of skate plaza on the Schuylkill River banks below the Philadelphia Museum of Art, conceived by the Franklin's Paine Skatepark Fund in 2002 and opened in 2013.
heads_up: Shared public space next to the river trail, with food trucks and events at times — keep an eye out for walkers.

name: Pitcher Park Memorial Skate Park
why: Grindline-built park of about 17,000 sq ft in Carnegie Park, the largest concrete skatepark in the Pittsburgh area, with a 20-ft-diameter full pipe between two bowls and a flowing street section.
heads_up: Directly off the Parkway West and I-79 and reachable by public transit from Pittsburgh.

name: Woodward Pennsylvania (Open Ride Sessions)
why: The original Woodward action-sports camp, running in central Pennsylvania for about 50 years; outside summer camp it sells public open-ride days on select weekends, with the indoor parks open on the late-autumn dates.
heads_up: Not drop-in: buy open-ride access online in advance; certified helmets are required and minors must be with an adult.

name: Jamestown Skatepark
why: Island park on Conanicut Island built in the early 2000s, with a double bowl joined by a spine, pool and steel coping, hips and pockets, plus a pyramid and a vert wall.
heads_up: Jamestown is reached by bridge from Newport or North Kingstown; the bowls are the draw.

name: Old Mountain Field Skatepark
why: Open since 2000 and added to over the years, this Peace Dale park mixes a long street course (rails, flat bars, pole jams, ledges, stairs) with a pool-style bowl that has a shallow and a deep end.
heads_up: Inside the Old Mountain Field sports complex on Kingstown Road in Peace Dale.

name: Buckwalter Skate Park
why: Beaufort County's 11,000-square-foot concrete park at the Buckwalter Recreation Center, opened in March 2010, designed by Pillar Design Studios and built by Artisan Skateparks from residents' suggestions.
heads_up: Parking and restrooms are shared with the Buckwalter Recreation Center.

name: Piney Mountain Bike Lounge
why: A mellow pump track of rollers and berms at a bike lounge with beer and food trucks. It is lit, so riding carries on after dark, and staff are on hand to give tips.
heads_up: The lights stay on only while the lounge is open and staffed, so riding follows its hours.

name: Garner Street Park Skatepark
why: A 6,300-square-foot boomerang-shaped concrete park north of Nashville, built by Hunger Skateparks with the Kiwanis Club and opened in March 2024, with a bowl, mini ramp, street features and a skateable steel sculpture by local fabricator Adam Heffner.
heads_up: Small park; Garner Street Park has restrooms and a shelter beside it.

name: Two Rivers Skatepark (Metro Nashville Skatepark)
why: Built by Metro Parks in 2004 with Wally Hollyday as designer, this 22,000-square-foot park in Two Rivers Park has a 10-foot combi pool with pool coping (the General Jackson), a mid-sized flow bowl and a street area.
heads_up: Open year-round from dawn to 11 p.m.; skateboards, inline skates and BMX share the park.

name: Heath Eiland and Morgan Moss BMX Skate Park (House Park)
why: Designed by New Line Skateparks and opened June 16, 2011 next to House Park, this 30,000 sq ft park replaced the old Green Park ramps with a bowl, a street plaza and skateable public art by Chris Levack.
heads_up: Shared with BMX riders, and the site sits in a flood plain, so check conditions after heavy rain.

name: Lee and Joe Jamail Skatepark
why: Designed by Grindline and Clark Condon and opened in 2008 in Buffalo Bayou Park, this in-ground park has one of the largest cradles in the country, a kidney pool and a 12.5-foot deep end; a $2.5 million renovation in 2016-17 added shade and seating.
heads_up: Skate it early on summer days, and after a Houston downpour give the bowls time to dry.

name: Mabel Davis Skate Park
why: Austin's first public skatepark, designed by Grindline and opened in late 2005: about 12,000 sq ft of technical concrete with a bowl of shallow and deep pockets and a street plaza with stairs, rails and a London gap.
heads_up: Built for advanced skaters; summer heat is intense, so evenings are best.

name: Paris Pump Track
why: An asphalt pump track on the Trail de Paris that hosted Red Bull UCI Pump Track World Championships qualifiers in May 2021 and July 2022.
heads_up: OpenStreetMap says it has no lights, so it's a daylight ride.

name: Andy "A_Dog" Williams Skatepark
why: A 21,000 sq ft waterfront park on Lake Champlain designed by Grindline and built by Artisan Skateparks in 2015, with a large central flow bowl, a mini bowl, a big vert bank and street lines.
heads_up: On the Burlington waterfront beside Lake Champlain — walkers and cyclists pass right by.

name: Talent Skatepark
why: Vermont's long-running indoor skatepark and shop, open since 2001 and reopened as a nonprofit in January 2020 after closing in 2018; sessions run in two-hour blocks year-round.
heads_up: Reserve a session online and sign a waiver first; helmets and sneakers required (rental helmets $5), and Saturday 10–12 is beginners only.

name: Charlottesville Skatepark
why: Charlottesville's city park, split into a transition side with several bowls and a separate street side with ledges, rails and stairs.
heads_up: Two parks in one — warm up on the street side before the bowls.

name: Lake Fairfax Skatepark
why: A 16,000 sq ft Spohn Ranch park opened in 2012 in Lake Fairfax Park, with a clover-shaped bowl with hips and a pocket and a street section with hubbas, handrails, stairs and a pole jam.
heads_up: Inside a Fairfax County park — check the county for hours and any entry rules before you go.

name: Mount Trashmore Skatepark
why: A 24,000 sq ft park in Mount Trashmore Park, opened in 2003 and rebuilt in 2007 after a fire, with a big street course, a 7-ft above-ground bowl and a competition vert ramp over 13 ft tall and 40 ft wide; Tony Hawk is among the pros who have skated it.
heads_up: Check the city's hours and any helmet or pass rules before you go.

name: Powhatan Springs Skatepark
why: A 17,000 sq ft Team Pain park in Arlington with an 11-ft kidney bowl, a 5-ft bowl, a snake run and a street section with handrails and a euro gap.
heads_up: The 11-ft kidney bowl is for confident bowl riders.

name: Texas Beach Skatepark
why: A DIY park built by local skaters and volunteers in the Texas Beach riverside area on the James River, reached from the North Bank Trail.
heads_up: DIY spot with no staff — skate at your own risk, and help keep it clean.

name: Warren County Skatepark
why: A 17,000 sq ft Pillar Design and Artisan Skateparks build in the Shenandoah Valley, with a pool-style bowl, a flow bowl with hips and a spine, and a street section with a vert quarter pipe.
heads_up: Front Royal sits at the north end of Skyline Drive, just off I-66.

name: Arlington Skate Park
why: Arlington's park off 188th Street NE is known for a large full pipe set inside a deep bowl.
heads_up: The full pipe and deep bowl are for confident riders.

name: Ballard Bowl
why: Rebuilt when Ballard Commons Park opened at the end of 2005, the unfenced 4,000 sq ft pool-style bowl keeps curves from the original 2,500 sq ft Ballard Bowl and has Penrose pool coping.
heads_up: A small, busy bowl with no lights; good for learning to pump transitions.

name: Battle Ground Skate & Bike Park
why: Ranked second on The Seattle Times' 2010 list as one of the state's largest parks, Battle Ground's park at East Main Street pairs street features with a deep bowl and an over-vert cradle.
heads_up: Shared with bikes, so look before you drop in.

name: Delridge Skatepark
why: A 13,000 sq ft Grindline park in West Seattle with ledges, rails, stairs and a manual pad next to a defined pool area and a flowing transition section.
heads_up: A good mix for street and bowl skaters in one stop.

name: Erickson Skate Park
why: Dreamland Skateparks built Port Angeles' park at East Fourth and South Race streets in 2005, with three bowls of different depths and shapes.
heads_up: Bowl-only terrain, with no street section.

name: Forks Skatepark
why: Grindline built Forks' park on Tillicum Lane with a mosaic-tiled bowl, a free-floating quarterpipe, brick banks and a street line.
heads_up: On the rainy Olympic Peninsula, so expect damp concrete outside summer.

name: Hillyard Skatepark
why: Built by Grindline in 2003 as one of Spokane's first dedicated skateparks, the 12,000 sq ft park has a long, undulating snake run, drop-ins, quarterpipes and bowls, and hosted a Tony Hawk tour stop in 2012.
heads_up: Lit for night sessions and regularly voted Spokane's best park, so it gets busy.

name: I-5 Colonnade Mountain Bike Park
why: Seattle's urban mountain bike park in I-5 Colonnade Park, under the freeway. Seattle Parks and the Evergreen Mountain Bike Alliance planned to rebuild its Tqalu Skills Zone with two paved pump tracks.
heads_up: The paved pump tracks were set for construction in summer–fall 2024; check Seattle Parks to see whether they have opened.

name: Jefferson Park Skatepark
why: Designed by Grindline with The Berger Partnership and opened in January 2012 behind the Jefferson Park Community Center on Beacon Hill, it has the deepest bowl in Seattle, shallower bowls, street features and a raised hexagonal dish.
heads_up: Lit for night sessions, with one of the best city views of any Seattle park.

name: Leavenworth Pump Track
why: An asphalt pump track built by Velosolutions that hosted Red Bull Pump Track World Championship qualifiers in 2018 and 2019.
heads_up: OpenStreetMap says it has no lights, so plan to ride in daylight.

name: Lower Woodland Skatepark
why: Opened in 2008 in Woodland Park near Green Lake as a regional park to ease crowding at the Ballard Bowl, the 17,000 sq ft park mixes a street area with several bowls.
heads_up: Woodland Park is open 4 a.m. to 11:30 p.m.

name: Marginal Way Skatepark
why: Seattle skaters started this DIY under the SR 99 bridge at East Marginal Way and Hanford in 2004 and still pay for and maintain it; it now has four connected sections, a pool and a mosaic-tiled cradle.
heads_up: Skateboards only; steep walls and quick transitions make it no place to learn.

name: River City Skatepark
why: First conceived by three South Park high school students, this 4,000 sq ft community-driven park has a big circular snake run and a clover-shaped run with four doors.
heads_up: Small neighborhood park, so take turns in the runs.

name: Riverfront Skate and Wheels Park
why: Spokane built this 8,000 sq ft park in downtown Riverfront Park with public input to replace the demolished Under the Freeway DIY; a flatbar saved from UTF is its centerpiece, with a wallride and two bowls.
heads_up: Downtown park with lots of foot traffic around it.

name: Roxhill Skatepark
why: A 10,000 sq ft West Seattle street spot built around mellow banks, with bank-to-ledge and bump-to-flatbar lines and a Pier 7-style manual pad.
heads_up: Mellow terrain that suits newer street skaters.

name: Scott Stamnes Memorial Skatepark
why: Built in 2002 by Grindline and Dreamland on Mount Baker Road east of Eastsound, Orcas Island's concrete bowl was backed by Warren Miller and Hobie Alter and topped The Seattle Times' 2010 list of the state's best parks.
heads_up: On Orcas Island, so plan around Washington State Ferries times.

name: Seattle Center Skate Plaza
why: Opened in 2021 and designed by Grindline with Skate Like A Girl and local skaters, the plaza near Climate Pledge Arena carries pieces of the old SeaSk8 park, including Perri Howard's glass wallride and five bronze skater figures.
heads_up: A public alley splits it into two skate areas joined by a sidewalk, so watch for cars crossing.

name: Fayetteville Town Park Skatepark
why: A Grindline park in the New River Gorge town of Fayetteville, with a kidney bowl with stairs and pool coping, a flow bowl and a street section.
heads_up: Open sunrise to sunset; easy to pair with a trip to the New River Gorge.

name: Fort Neal Skatepark
why: A 10,000 sq ft Grindline park with a 6–10 ft clover bowl with pool coping and a full street section with stairs, handrails and a euro gap.
heads_up: Open sunrise to sunset.

name: Skatepark of Charleston
why: Downtown Charleston park under Interstate 64 with a mini ramp, quarter pipes, a spine, a pyramid, ledges and rails.
heads_up: Open 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.; the interstate overhead keeps it partly sheltered from rain.

name: Wheeling Skatepark
why: A 10,000 sq ft Grindline park built in 2007, with a 4–10 ft bowl with an island, hips and extensions, and a street section with stairs and rails.
heads_up: Listed as open 24/7, but there's no staff — skate with a friend after dark.

name: Four Seasons Skatepark
why: A warehouse indoor park of about 22,000 square feet of wooden ramps in the Menomonee River Valley, with street features, a flow bowl, mini ramps and a foam pit.
heads_up: Paid day passes or membership; helmets required.

name: Goodman Skatepark
why: Completed in 2017 in McPike Park for about $1.2 million, designed by Stantec and built by Hardcore Skateparks, with a vert bowl, a flow bowl and a street plaza.
heads_up: Open 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. in season and closed in winter.

name: The Turf Skatepark
why: Surfin' Turf opened in 1979 with five concrete pools designed by Art Kent and was later filled with gravel; Grindline rebuilt the five original bowls to their 1979 scale, plus a combi bowl and street course, and the city rededicated it on June 7, 2025.
heads_up: Rebuilt 1970s pool shapes, so expect old-school transitions; open dawn to dusk.

name: Wauwatosa Skate Park (Hart Park)
why: A free concrete park in Hart Park opened in 2015, with a triple bowl, a flow bowl, ledges, handrails, stairs and an A-frame.
heads_up: No helmet rule, but gear is recommended; Hart Park has restrooms and parking.
